stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with 6 months of amenorrhea and milky nipple discharge. She reports frequently bumping into people and door frames on both sides. Visual field testing shows loss of the temporal field in both eyes. Which retinal fibers are most likely compressed?

options.text: Uncrossed temporal retinal fibers from both eyes
Crossing nasal retinal fibers from both eyes at the optic chiasm
Both optic tracts
Left optic nerve only
Both lateral geniculate nuclei

explanation: Nasal retinal fibers (temporal visual fields) cross at the optic chiasm. Compression from below by a pituitary adenoma (here a prolactinoma: amenorrhea, galactorrhea) interrupts these crossing fibers, producing bitemporal hemianopia ("tunnel vision"). Temporal retinal fibers remain uncrossed and are spared at the chiasm.

stem: A 55-year-old man has an infarct in the left temporal lobe white matter and reports repeatedly striking his head on high cabinets because he does not see objects in the upper right part of his visual field with either eye. Visual field testing shows a right superior homonymous quadrantanopia. Which structure is most likely damaged?

options.text: Left optic tract
Left dorsal optic radiations in the parietal lobe
Right Meyer loop
Right cuneus
Left Meyer loop carrying fibers from the inferior retina

explanation: The lower retina sees the UPPER visual field. Inferior retinal fibers travel in the optic radiations through Meyer loop in the temporal lobe to the lingual gyrus (below the calcarine sulcus). A left temporal lesion causes a right superior homonymous quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky"). Dorsal radiations through parietal lobe carry superior retinal fibers (inferior quadrantanopia).

stem: A 24-year-old man repeatedly trips over his dog when it is on his right side. MRI shows a lesion in the left parietal white matter, and visual field testing shows a right inferior homonymous quadrantanopia. Which structure is most likely damaged?

options.text: Left Meyer loop in the temporal lobe
Left optic tract bordering crus cerebri
Left superior optic radiations in parietal lobe
Right superior optic radiations in parietal lobe
Left lingual gyrus bordering calcarine sulcus

explanation: Superior retinal fibers (seeing the lower field) run in the dorsal optic radiations through the parietal lobe to the cuneus, above the calcarine sulcus. A left parietal lesion causes a right inferior homonymous quadrantanopia ("pie on the floor"): patients trip over objects below eye level.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation suddenly cannot see anything to her left but can still read the central letters on an eye chart. Visual field testing shows a left homonymous hemianopia with sparing of the central 10 degrees. Pupillary light reflexes are normal. Occlusion of which artery is most likely?

options.text: Left posterior cerebral artery
Left middle cerebral artery
Right middle cerebral artery
Right posterior cerebral artery
Right anterior cerebral artery

explanation: Left homonymous hemianopia localizes to the right occipital lobe or optic tract/radiations. Macular sparing indicates a cortical (calcarine) lesion: the large macular representation at the occipital pole has dual blood supply (PCA plus MCA collaterals), so it is spared by PCA occlusion. Pupillary light responses are normal because reflex fibers leave the optic tract before the LGN to reach the pretectal area.

stem: An 8-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis and poor adherence to pancreatic enzyme and vitamin supplementation reports difficulty seeing in dim light and at dusk. Which cell type and process are most likely impaired?

options.text: Cones; reduced cone opsin synthesis
Rods; reduced rhodopsin synthesis
Bipolar cells; reduced glutamate release
Retinal ganglion cells; reduced action potential generation
Muller glia; reduced potassium buffering

explanation: Vitamin A is needed to synthesize rhodopsin (and cone opsins). Rods are highly light-sensitive, mediate black-and-white vision in dim light, and are peripheral, so vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness first. Cones (fovea, color, acuity) are affected later.

stem: In an experimental preparation, intracellular recordings are made from different retinal neurons during a light flash. Which cell type is the first in the visual pathway to generate action potentials, and how do photoreceptors respond to light?

options.text: Ganglion cells; photoreceptors hyperpolarize in light
Bipolar cells; photoreceptors hyperpolarize in light
Ganglion cells; photoreceptors depolarize in light
Photoreceptors; they depolarize in light
Bipolar cells; photoreceptors depolarize in light

explanation: Photoreceptors are depolarized in the dark (releasing glutamate) and hyperpolarize in response to light; they do not generate action potentials. Bipolar cells also use graded potentials. Retinal ganglion cells are the first neurons in the pathway to fire action potentials; their axons form the optic nerve.

stem: An 8-year-old has headaches after reading and difficulty focusing on near work, though distance vision is relatively good. Cycloplegic refraction shows the image of a distant object focuses behind the retina. Which is the most likely cause and correction?

options.text: Eye too long or refractive power too strong; concave lens
Eye too short or refractive power too weak; convex lens
Unequal corneal curvature across meridians; cylindrical lens
Age-related lens stiffening; positive reading glasses
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment; pneumatic retinopexy

explanation: Hyperopia: the eyeball is too short (or refractive power too weak), so the image focuses behind the retina. Correction: convex (converging) lens. Children may accommodate, causing eyestrain and headaches with near work.

stem: A 14-year-old cannot read the blackboard but reads a book comfortably. Light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina. Which is the most likely cause and correction?

options.text: Eye too short with focal point behind retina; convex lens
Unequal corneal curvature across meridians; cylindrical lens
Eye too long with focal point in front of retina; concave lens
Stiff crystalline lens with decreased near focus; bifocals
Autoimmune optic nerve demyelination; intravenous steroids

explanation: Myopia: the eye is too long (or the cornea too curved), so distant images focus in front of the retina. Correction: concave (diverging) lens.

stem: A 47-year-old emmetropic woman reports she must hold menus at arm's length to read. Distance vision is normal. Which mechanism is responsible?

options.text: Asymmetric corneal curvature across principal meridians
Shortened axial eyeball length focusing behind the fovea
Drusen deposition in the macular retinal pigment layer
Age-related lens stiffening with loss of accommodation
Elongated axial globe length focusing anterior to retina

explanation: Presbyopia: with age the lens stiffens and the ciliary muscle's effect on lens shape decreases, so near-focusing (accommodation) fails and the near image focuses behind the retina. Treated with reading glasses (convex lenses).

stem: A 30-year-old reports blurred vision at all distances. Keratometry shows different corneal curvature along different meridians. Which describes the problem and its correction?

options.text: Excess axial globe length; concave spherical lens
Shortened axial globe length; convex spherical lens
Loss of crystalline lens elasticity; bifocal reading lenses
Peripheral retinal tear; argon laser barrier retinopexy
Unequal curvature across meridians; cylindrical lens

explanation: Astigmatism: unequal curvature of the cornea (or lens) in different meridians causes blur at all distances. Corrected with a cylindrical lens.

stem: A patient undergoes LASIK to reshape the front of the eye and change his refractive error. Which structure contributes the most refractive power of the eye and is therefore the target?

options.text: Crystalline lens
Corneal surface
Vitreous humor
Aqueous humor
Retinal layer

explanation: The cornea provides about two-thirds of the eye's refractive power at the air-cornea interface; the lens adds the adjustable remainder. LASIK reshapes the cornea.

stem: Which structure produces aqueous humor and also contains the muscle that adjusts lens shape during accommodation?

options.text: Choroid
Iris stroma
Ciliary body
Lens epithelium
Retinal pigment epithelium

explanation: The ciliary body secretes aqueous humor (ciliary processes) and contains the ciliary muscle that, via zonular fibers, changes lens shape for accommodation.

stem: During visual field testing, a normal person has a small area of absent vision in the temporal field of each eye. Which structure corresponds to this physiologic blind spot?

options.text: Fovea centralis
Macula lutea
Ora serrata
Vitreous base
Optic nerve disc

explanation: The physiologic blind spot corresponds to the optic disc, where ganglion cell axons exit the retina and there are no photoreceptors. It lies in the temporal visual field about 15 degrees from fixation. The fovea is the point of highest acuity.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has headaches and vomiting. Fundoscopy shows bilateral optic disc swelling; visual fields show enlarged blind spots with normal acuity. Which mechanism underlies the disc swelling?

options.text: Elevated intracranial pressure transmitted along optic nerve sheath
Autoimmune demyelinating inflammation of intraorbital optic nerve
Acute embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery bifurcation
Extracellular drusen accumulation beneath retinal pigment layer
Glaucomatous axonal death with progressive optic nerve cupping

explanation: Papilledema is optic disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure, transmitted along the optic nerve sheath and impairing axoplasmic flow. The enlarged blind spot reflects peripapillary retinal displacement; acuity is usually normal until late.

stem: A rod photoreceptor absorbs a photon of light. Which intracellular event follows?

options.text: Sustained elevation in cytoplasmic cGMP levels opening cation channels
Activation of transducin and PDE, closing cGMP-gated sodium channels
Opening of voltage-dependent L-type calcium channels across terminal
Increased tonic release of glutamate onto postsynaptic bipolar cells
Direct dephosphorylation and opening of cGMP-activated sodium channels

explanation: Light converts 11-cis-retinal to all-trans in rhodopsin, activating transducin, which activates phosphodiesterase (PDE). cGMP falls, cGMP-gated Na+ channels close, the cell hyperpolarizes, and glutamate release decreases.

stem: A 14-year-old has photophobia, poor central acuity, and abnormal color vision, but night vision is normal. Which cells are primarily affected?

options.text: Rods
Cones
Ganglion cells
Retinal pigment epithelium
Muller cells

explanation: Cone dystrophy: loss of cone function causes photophobia, reduced central acuity, and abnormal color vision, with preserved night vision (rods). Cones are concentrated in the fovea and mediate bright-light and color vision.

stem: A 30-year-old man cannot distinguish red from green. His maternal uncle has the same difficulty. What is the likely inheritance pattern?

options.text: Autosomal dominant
Autosomal recessive
X-linked recessive
Mitochondrial
Y-linked

explanation: Red-green color blindness is X-linked recessive (opsin genes on X), so it affects males much more often and is passed via carrier mothers (e.g., affected maternal uncle).

stem: Which function of the retinal pigment epithelium is critical for photoreceptor health?

options.text: Secreting aqueous humor into the posterior chamber
Phagocytosing shed outer segments and recycling retinal
Propagating all-or-none action potentials to optic chiasm
Refracting incident light rays directly onto the fovea
Synthesizing hyaluronic acid for the vitreous matrix

explanation: The RPE phagocytoses the shed tips of photoreceptor outer segments daily and regenerates 11-cis-retinal (visual cycle); it also forms part of the blood-retina barrier. RPE or Bruch membrane dysfunction contributes to AMD.

stem: Incoming light must pass through which retinal cells and layers before reaching the photoreceptor outer segments?

options.text: Ganglion cell layer and bipolar cells
Photoreceptors first
Retinal pigment epithelium first
Choroid first
Sclera only

explanation: The retina is inverted: light passes through the ganglion cell layer and bipolar cells (and nerve fiber layer) before reaching photoreceptors. The fovea minimizes this by displacing inner layers aside.

stem: A 62-year-old woman has progressive painless central vision loss in her right eye; the left eye is normal. Visual field testing shows constriction of the right eye only. Where is the lesion most likely located?

options.text: Right optic nerve prior to chiasm
Central crossing optic chiasm
Contralateral left optic tract
Right parietal optic radiations
Right calcarine occipital cortex

explanation: Monocular visual loss indicates a lesion anterior to the optic chiasm (retina or optic nerve). Lesions at or beyond the chiasm affect both eyes.

stem: A 58-year-old man has a right homonymous hemianopia with incongruous defects in the two eyes and no macular sparing. Which lesion is most likely?

options.text: Left optic tract
Left occipital pole
Right optic tract
Optic chiasm
Left optic nerve

explanation: Optic tract lesions cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia, typically incongruous and without macular sparing (macular fibers are tightly bundled with the rest). A left optic tract lesion causes right hemianopia. Occipital pole lesions would be congruous.

stem: Which lesion location produces homonymous field defects that are most nearly identical in the two eyes (congruous)?

options.text: Optic nerve
Optic chiasm
Optic tract
Occipital cortex
Retina

explanation: Congruity increases posteriorly: tract lesions are incongruous, radiations less so, and occipital cortex lesions yield the most congruous (nearly identical) homonymous defects, often with macular sparing.

stem: A pituitary macroadenoma grows upward and compresses the optic chiasm from below. Which is the earliest typical visual field deficit?

options.text: Superior bitemporal quadrantanopia
Inferior bitemporal quadrantanopia
Binasal hemianopia
Right homonymous hemianopia
Central scotoma

explanation: Fibers from the inferior nasal retina (seeing the superior temporal field) cross in the lower anterior chiasm and are compressed first by pituitary tumors from below, giving a superior bitemporal quadrantanopia that progresses to bitemporal hemianopia. Craniopharyngioma, compressing from above, causes inferior defects first.

stem: A 70-year-old man has bilateral atherosclerotic calcified internal carotid arteries that compress the lateral aspects of the optic chiasm. Which visual field defect results?

options.text: Bitemporal hemianopia
Right homonymous hemianopia
Binasal hemianopia
Monocular blindness
Central scotoma

explanation: The uncrossed temporal retinal fibers (nasal field) run laterally in the chiasm; compression from both sides by dilated or calcified internal carotids produces binasal hemianopia (rare).

stem: A 60-year-old man with a right parietal tumor has a left inferior homonymous quadrantanopia. Which fibers are interrupted?

options.text: Right Meyer loop in the temporal lobe
Right dorsal optic radiations in parietal lobe
Left dorsal optic radiations in parietal lobe
Right lingual gyrus along the calcarine
Left optic tract bordering cerebral peduncle

explanation: Right dorsal (parietal) optic radiations carry superior retinal fibers from the left visual field's inferior part; damage causes a left inferior homonymous quadrantanopia. Meyer loop lesions cause superior quadrantanopia.

stem: A 70-year-old man after a basilar top embolus has bilateral occipital infarcts. He insists he can see, but bumps into objects. Which exam finding best distinguishes cortical blindness from blindness due to bilateral optic nerve disease?

options.text: Preserved pupillary light reflexes and normal fundi
Bilateral relative afferent pupillary defects
Optic atrophy
Absent consensual light reflex
Papilledema

explanation: In cortical blindness the retinas, optic nerves, and the pupillary light reflex pathway (which bypasses cortex via the pretectal area) are intact, so pupillary reflexes and fundi are normal. Patients may deny their blindness (Anton syndrome).

stem: A 52-year-old man has a right occipital infarct involving the cuneus (above the calcarine fissure). Which visual deficit is expected?

options.text: Left inferior quadrantanopia
Left superior quadrantanopia
Right inferior quadrantanopia
Right superior quadrantanopia
Left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

explanation: The cuneus (above the calcarine fissure) receives superior retinal fibers (inferior visual field); the lingual gyrus (below) receives inferior retinal fibers (superior field). A right cuneus lesion causes a left inferior quadrantanopia.

stem: A gunshot wound destroys the left occipital pole, producing a right homonymous hemianopia WITHOUT macular sparing. Which best explains the lack of sparing?

options.text: The fovea projects exclusively through the ipsilateral optic tract
Direct destruction of occipital pole foveal visual representation
Foveal ganglion axons project bilaterally to both occipital lobes
Total ischemic necrosis of the lateral geniculate relay nucleus
Traumatic complete transection of the ipsilateral optic nerve

explanation: The macula has a disproportionately large cortical representation at the occipital pole, with dual blood supply (PCA and MCA branches). Direct trauma destroys the pole, abolishing macular representation, whereas a PCA infarct spares it via MCA collateral supply.

stem: After bilateral occipitotemporal infarcts, a 66-year-old man can describe facial features and has normal visual acuity but does not recognize his wife until she speaks. Which is the best diagnosis?

options.text: Cortical blindness from bilateral calcarine sulcus infarction
Hemispatial neglect from non-dominant parietal lobe injury
Prosopagnosia from bilateral fusiform gyrus damage
Anton visual anosognosia from striate cortex infarction
Pure alexia without agraphia from splenium infarction

explanation: Visual agnosia: perception is intact but association cortex (inferior temporal-occipital, fusiform area) cannot interpret what is seen. Prosopagnosia is inability to recognize faces; patients identify the person by voice.

stem: Branch occlusion of the retinal artery supplying the INFERIOR half of the left retina causes which visual field deficit?

options.text: Superior altitudinal visual defect in the left eye
Inferior altitudinal visual defect in the left eye
Bitemporal hemianopic visual field defect in both eyes
Monocular central scotoma in the affected left eye
Homonymous hemianopia affecting the right visual field

explanation: The optic system inverts images: the inferior retina sees the superior visual field. Loss of the inferior half of one retina causes a superior altitudinal defect in that eye.

stem: Light from the RIGHT visual hemifield strikes which retinal regions, and which hemisphere's occipital cortex processes it?

options.text: Nasal retina of the right eye and temporal retina of the left eye; left occipital cortex
Temporal retina of the right eye and nasal retina of the left eye; right occipital cortex
Nasal retina of both eyes; right occipital cortex
Temporal retina of both eyes; left occipital cortex
Right eye only; right occipital cortex

explanation: The right hemifield falls on the nasal retina of the right eye and the temporal retina of the left eye. Nasal fibers cross at the chiasm and temporal fibers do not, so both converge in the left optic tract and left occipital cortex.

stem: A 70-year-old man has sudden fluent speech that makes no sense, poor comprehension, and a right superior homonymous quadrantanopia. Which vessel territory is most likely involved?

options.text: Left anterior cerebral artery
Left posterior cerebral artery
Right middle cerebral artery, inferior division
Left middle cerebral artery, inferior division
Basilar artery

explanation: The inferior division of the left MCA supplies the temporal lobe: Wernicke area (fluent aphasia with poor comprehension) and Meyer loop of the optic radiations (right superior quadrantanopia).

stem: In the primary visual pathway, which neurons are the fourth-order neurons?

options.text: Photoreceptor outer segments
Retinal bipolar interneurons
Retinal ganglion projection cells
Lateral geniculate relay neurons
Pretectal olivary nucleus cells

explanation: Visual pathway order: photoreceptors (1st), bipolar cells (2nd), retinal ganglion cells (3rd), LGN neurons (4th), which project via the optic radiations to primary visual cortex.

stem: A patient with macular disease has difficulty reading and recognizing faces but retains peripheral vision. Which retinal region, composed predominantly of cones and responsible for the highest visual acuity, is most affected?

options.text: Optic disc
Fovea centralis
Ora serrata
Peripheral retina
Pars plana

explanation: The fovea centralis (center of the macula) contains only cones and mediates highest visual acuity and color vision. Macular disease (e.g., AMD) causes central scotoma and trouble reading and recognizing faces.

stem: In a kitten, one eyelid is sutured shut during the first weeks of life. After it is reopened, vision in that eye remains poor despite a normal retina. Which cortical change explains this?

options.text: Deprived eye loses cortical synaptic territory in ocular dominance columns
Extensive apoptotic death of retinal ganglion cells in the deprived eye
Selective proliferative sprouting of LGN neurons serving the closed eye
Total preservation of physiological binocular cortical response profiles
Permanent irreversible crystalline lens clouding from lack of light

explanation: Hubel and Wiesel: during the critical period, monocular deprivation shifts cortical ocular dominance columns toward the open eye; the deprived eye loses cortical representation, causing amblyopia even with a normal retina. Clinical analog: unilateral congenital cataract.

stem: A malnourished child has dry, wrinkled conjunctiva with foamy gray patches (Bitot spots) and corneal softening. Deficiency of which vitamin is most likely?

options.text: Vitamin C
Vitamin A
Vitamin E
Niacin
Vitamin B12

explanation: Vitamin A deficiency: night blindness, xerophthalmia, Bitot spots (keratinized conjunctival plaques), and keratomalacia. Vitamin A is needed for rhodopsin and for epithelial integrity.

stem: A 66-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history has 3 months of right shoulder and arm pain. Examination shows right ptosis, a smaller right pupil that dilates poorly in the dark, and decreased sweating on the right side of the face. Compression of which structure best explains his ocular findings?

options.text: Right oculomotor nerve in cavernous sinus
Right postganglionic ciliary ganglion
Right cervical sympathetic chain at lung apex
Right pretectal Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Right intraorbital optic nerve trunk

explanation: Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) from a Pancoast tumor at the lung apex. The sympathetic dilation pathway has three neurons: hypothalamus, intermediolateral cell column (T1-T2), superior cervical ganglion, with postganglionic fibers along the internal carotid and long ciliary nerves to the dilator pupillae. Interruption causes unopposed parasympathetic miosis. CN III and ciliary ganglion lesions cause mydriasis.

stem: A 57-year-old man with hypertension develops right ptosis and a constricted right pupil. He also has decreased pain and temperature sensation over the left arm, trunk, and leg. MRI shows a lesion in the right lateral brainstem. Which best explains the combination of findings?

options.text: Right oculomotor nucleus lesion with adjacent corticospinal tract involvement
Right lateral brainstem lesion involving descending sympathetic and spinothalamic tracts
Right superior cervical ganglion lesion with sympathetic postganglionic denervation
Right cavernous sinus mass lesion involving oculomotor and ophthalmic divisions
Right midbrain tegmental lesion affecting the visceral Edinger-Westphal nucleus

explanation: The first-order descending sympathetic (hypothalamospinal) fibers run ipsilaterally in the lateral brainstem tegmentum next to the spinothalamic system. A lateral medullary lesion produces ipsilateral Horner syndrome plus contralateral loss of pain and temperature from the body (spinothalamic fibers have already crossed).

stem: A 61-year-old man with long-standing diabetes and hypertension wakes with double vision and right ptosis. The right eye is deviated down and out. The right pupil is 3 mm and briskly reactive to light. He has no headache and imaging is unremarkable. Which best explains the preserved pupillary light reflex?

options.text: Pupillary parasympathetic fibers travel via the trochlear nerve rather than CN III
Sympathetic pupillomotor tone actively constricts the pupil during ischemic events
Visceral Edinger-Westphal preganglionic neurons lie isolated from midbrain complexes
Superficial parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers are relatively spared by core ischemia
Pupillary constriction is mediated directly by optic nerve collaterals bypassing CN III

explanation: Microvascular (ischemic) CN III palsy in diabetes classically spares the pupil: parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers lie on the outer surface of the nerve with collateral blood supply, while the central motor fibers are more vulnerable to ischemia. Compressive lesions (PComm aneurysm, uncal herniation) affect the peripheral fibers first, causing a blown pupil.

stem: After a motorcycle accident, a 25-year-old man has loss of vision in one eye. When a light is shone in his right eye, neither pupil constricts. When a light is shone in his left eye, both pupils constrict briskly. Eye movements and eyelid position are normal. Which structure is most likely damaged?

options.text: Right oculomotor nerve
Left optic nerve
Right optic tract
Right pretectal area
Right optic nerve

explanation: The right optic nerve is the afferent limb for light in the right eye: stimulation produces neither direct nor consensual response, while light in the intact left eye elicits both. A right CN III lesion would give a consensual response in the left eye with light in the right eye but no right pupil constriction with light in either eye, plus ptosis and abnormal eye movements.

stem: A 29-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has double vision when looking to the right. On attempted rightward gaze, her left eye fails to adduct while the right eye abducts with nystagmus. Leftward gaze is normal. Both eyes converge normally when she follows a finger toward her nose. Which is the most likely location of the lesion?

options.text: Right medial longitudinal fasciculus
Left medial longitudinal fasciculus
Left abducens nucleus
Right paramedian pontine reticular formation
Left oculomotor nerve

explanation: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a left MLF lesion. The MLF carries axons from abducens interneurons to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus. On right gaze, the left MLF fails to relay the signal, so the left eye cannot adduct (abducting nystagmus in the right eye). Convergence is spared because that pathway bypasses the pons/MLF. MS is a classic cause in young adults.

stem: A 72-year-old man has sudden right hemiparesis and aphasia. CT shows an acute left middle cerebral artery infarct involving the left frontal eye field. Which resting eye position is most likely?

options.text: Deviated to the right
Deviated upward
Deviated to the left
Deviated downward
Midline with normal conjugate gaze

explanation: Each frontal eye field drives the eyes to the contralateral side. A stroke destroys the left FEF, leaving the right FEF unopposed, so the eyes deviate toward the lesion (left). A seizure irritating one FEF drives the eyes away from the lesion. Rule: stroke = toward lesion; seizure = away. (PPRF lesions cause deviation AWAY from the lesion.)

stem: A 47-year-old man presents with 6 days of left periorbital pain and swelling, fever, and a swollen gum from a dental infection. Examination shows left proptosis, a closed edematous eyelid, an absent left corneal reflex, limited eye movements in all directions, and a sluggish left pupillary response. MRI shows a dilated venous sinus with filling defects. Thrombosis of which structure is most likely, and which nerves pass through it?

options.text: Cavernous sinus; CN III, IV, VI, V2, V3
Superior sagittal sinus; CN I and II
Sigmoid sinus; CN IX, X, XI
Cavernous sinus; CN III, IV, VI, V1, V2
Superior ophthalmic vein only; CN II

explanation: Facial and dental infections spread through valveless facial and ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus (septic thrombosis). The sinus contains CN III, IV, VI, V1, V2 (plus ICA and sympathetic plexus), so thrombosis causes ophthalmoplegia, diminished corneal reflex (V1), sluggish pupil, proptosis, and periorbital edema. A medical emergency.

stem: A light is shone into a patient's right eye, and the LEFT pupil constricts. Which sequence correctly traces the pathway that produces this consensual response?

options.text: Optic nerve, LGN, visual cortex, contralateral Edinger-Westphal, CN III
Optic nerve, pretectal area, both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, CN III, ciliary ganglion
Optic nerve, superior colliculus, contralateral CN IV, sphincter pupillae
Optic nerve, hypothalamus, thoracic IML, superior cervical ganglion, dilator
Optic nerve, ipsilateral Edinger-Westphal only, ipsilateral ciliary ganglion

explanation: Light reflex: retina, optic nerve, pretectal area (which projects bilaterally), both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, CN III, ciliary ganglion, sphincter pupillae. The bilateral projection produces the consensual response. The cortex is not required.

stem: A 66-year-old woman has an infarct of the right lateral geniculate nucleus causing a left homonymous hemianopia. Her pupillary light reflexes are normal. Which best explains the preserved light reflex?

options.text: The pupillary light reflex requires only direct motor CN III input
The pupillary light reflex is mediated entirely by superior colliculus
Pupillary afferents exit before the LGN to synapse in pretectal nuclei
The sympathetic pupillary dilator pathway compensates for the loss
Crossing decussating fibers from the contralateral retina compensate

explanation: Retinal afferents for the pupillary reflex exit the optic tract before the LGN and project to the pretectal area, so LGN, optic radiation, and cortical lesions leave the light reflex intact despite visual field loss.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has acute optic neuritis of the right eye. On the swinging flashlight test, when the light moves from the left eye to the right eye, both pupils dilate. Which is the best interpretation?

options.text: Right afferent pupillary defect from reduced optic nerve conduction
Right oculomotor nerve palsy with complete internal ophthalmoplegia
Left Horner syndrome from disruption of sympathetic innervation
Right Adie tonic pupil with denervation cholinergic sensitivity
Normal physiological pupillary response with symmetric light reflex

explanation: A relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn): the swinging flashlight shows paradoxical dilation when light moves to the eye with the damaged afferent limb (reduced afferent signal), even though the efferent pathway is intact.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has 3 days of right eye pain that worsens with eye movement, reduced visual acuity, and desaturation of colors. She has a right relative afferent pupillary defect. Which underlying process is most likely?

options.text: Ischemic infarction of the optic nerve head
Pituitary adenoma compressing chiasmal crossing fibers
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment across the macula
Demyelinating optic neuritis linked to multiple sclerosis
Acute closed-angle glaucoma with severe corneal edema

explanation: Optic neuritis: eye pain with movement, decreased acuity, color desaturation, RAPD. The optic nerve is a CNS tract myelinated by oligodendrocytes; demyelination (often MS) is the cause. Treated with IV methylprednisolone.

stem: A 32-year-old woman notices a dilated left pupil that constricts poorly to light but slowly and tonically to near effort. Her patellar reflexes are diminished bilaterally. Which structure is most likely damaged?

options.text: Superior cervical sympathetic ganglion
Ciliary ganglion and short ciliary nerves
Optic nerve fibers at the orbital apex
Oculomotor trunk within the cavernous sinus
Cervical paravertebral sympathetic chain

explanation: Adie tonic pupil: postganglionic parasympathetic denervation (ciliary ganglion/short ciliary nerves) causes a dilated pupil with poor, slow constriction to light and tonic constriction to near; often with diminished deep tendon reflexes. Typically a young woman.

stem: While reading, a person's ciliary muscle contracts. Which change results?

options.text: Zonular fibers tighten and the lens flattens for distance
Iris dilator contracts producing pupillary mydriasis
Zonular fibers relax and the lens rounds up for near focus
Ciliary epithelium increases aqueous humor secretion
Vitreous gel contracts reducing internal ocular volume

explanation: Ciliary muscle contraction relaxes the zonular fibers, allowing the elastic lens to become rounder and increasing refractive power for near vision (accommodation). With age, the lens stiffens (presbyopia).

stem: A 30-year-old has bilateral occipital lobe damage from trauma. His pupils constrict normally to direct light, but he cannot accommodate when looking at a near object. Which best explains this dissociation?

options.text: Accommodation requires visual cortical processing, whereas light reflex bypasses cortex
Direct light reflex requires cortical occipital processing, whereas near reflex does not
Both oculomotor nerve trunks suffered incomplete partial axonal shearing injuries
Bilateral ciliary ganglia suffered ischemic postganglionic parasympathetic damage
Sympathetic pupillary pathways suffered traumatic injury along the cervical cord

explanation: The accommodation reflex requires the visual cortex to process the blurred near image before descending to the pretectal area and Edinger-Westphal nucleus, then CN III. The light reflex bypasses the cortex, so it remains intact.

stem: A 38-year-old woman develops neck pain followed by right ptosis and miosis after a chiropractic manipulation. Facial sweating is preserved. Which neuron of the sympathetic pathway to the eye is most likely interrupted?

options.text: First-order (hypothalamospinal) neuron
Second-order (preganglionic) neuron at the lung apex
Third-order (postganglionic) neuron along the internal carotid artery
Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Oculomotor nerve

explanation: Carotid artery dissection damages the third-order (postganglionic) sympathetic fibers that travel with the internal carotid, giving ptosis and miosis but preserved facial sweating (sweat fibers follow the external carotid). Pain in the neck or face is common.

stem: A 50-year-old man has anisocoria that is greater in dim light than in bright light, with mild ptosis on the side of the smaller pupil. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Horner syndrome
Compressive CN III palsy
Adie tonic pupil
Atropine instillation
Optic neuritis

explanation: Horner syndrome: the smaller pupil fails to dilate (dilation lag), so anisocoria is greater in the dark. In CN III palsy or Adie pupil, the larger pupil fails to constrict, so anisocoria is greater in bright light.

stem: Cocaine eye drops fail to dilate a patient's right pupil but dilate the left normally. Which best explains why this confirms Horner syndrome?

options.text: Cocaine acts as a direct alpha-1 adrenergic agonist on dilator pupillae
Cocaine acts as a competitive muscarinic antagonist on sphincter pupillae
Cocaine directly stimulates nicotinic and muscarinic cholinergic receptors
Cocaine blocks norepinephrine reuptake, requiring intact tonic basal release
Cocaine directly stimulates rapid release of vesicular norepinephrine pools

explanation: Cocaine blocks norepinephrine reuptake at the synapse; in a normal pupil, released NE accumulates and dilates the pupil. In Horner syndrome (any level), insufficient NE is released, so the pupil fails to dilate.

stem: A farmer exposed to organophosphate insecticide has miosis, salivation, lacrimation, and bradycardia. Which receptor mediates the constriction of the pupil?

options.text: Alpha-1 receptors on the dilator pupillae
M3 muscarinic receptors on the sphincter pupillae
Nicotinic receptors on the iris
Beta-2 receptors on the ciliary body
Dopamine D1 receptors

explanation: Pupillary constriction is mediated by acetylcholine acting on M3 muscarinic receptors on the sphincter pupillae. Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing excess ACh and miosis. Dilation uses alpha-1 receptors on the dilator pupillae.

stem: A 25-year-old has a dilated unreactive pupil with normal eye movements and no ptosis. After 1% pilocarpine drops the pupil does not constrict. He recently handled a plant containing scopolamine. Which is the most likely interpretation?

options.text: Pharmacologic blockade by muscarinic antagonist drops
Parasympathetic denervation with Adie tonic pupil
Mechanical uncal herniation with compressive CN III palsy
Oculosympathetic disruption causing Horner syndrome
Demyelinating inflammation causing acute optic neuritis

explanation: A pupil that fails to constrict to pilocarpine indicates receptor blockade (anticholinergics such as scopolamine/atropine, or angel's trumpet). A compressive CN III palsy constricts to pilocarpine; an Adie tonic pupil constricts to dilute pilocarpine from denervation hypersensitivity.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has a sudden, severe 'worst headache of her life' followed by right ptosis, a dilated fixed pupil, and the right eye deviated down and out. Which is the most likely cause?

options.text: Diabetic microvascular infarction of CN III
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing CN III
Pancoast tumor
Multiple sclerosis plaque
Cavernous sinus thrombosis

explanation: Sudden severe headache with a CN III palsy involving the pupil suggests a posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing the superficial parasympathetic fibers. This is a neurosurgical emergency (impending subarachnoid hemorrhage).

stem: After head trauma with an expanding right epidural hematoma, a patient's right pupil dilates and becomes unreactive, followed by left hemiparesis. Which mechanism best explains the pupil?

options.text: Compression of CN III parasympathetic fibers by uncal herniation
Direct ischemic infarction of the contralateral oculomotor nucleus
Traumatic transection of sympathetic fibers in the cavernous sinus
Severe contusion of the ipsilateral optic nerve at the orbital canal
Contralateral uncal herniation compressing the cerebral peduncle

explanation: In uncal herniation, the medial temporal lobe (uncus) compresses the ipsilateral CN III against the tentorium; superficially located parasympathetic fibers are hit first, producing a blown pupil.

stem: A 63-year-old has a stroke in the dorsal caudal pons. Neither eye can look to the left, and he has left lower motor neuron facial weakness. Which structure is most likely damaged?

options.text: Left CN VI nerve
Left abducens nucleus
Right abducens nucleus
Left medial longitudinal fasciculus
Right frontal eye field

explanation: The abducens nucleus contains lateral rectus motoneurons and interneurons that project through the contralateral MLF to the oculomotor nucleus. A nuclear lesion causes an ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy (neither eye can look toward the lesion); facial nerve fibers loop around the nucleus (facial colliculus), explaining ipsilateral facial weakness. A CN VI nerve lesion affects only the ipsilateral lateral rectus.

stem: A 66-year-old man has a hemorrhage in the left paramedian pons involving the PPRF. Which is the most likely eye finding?

options.text: Eyes deviated to the left and unable to look right
Eyes deviated to the right and unable to look left
Eyes deviated upward
Left eye down and out
Midline eyes with an isolated adduction deficit

explanation: The PPRF drives horizontal gaze toward its own side. A left PPRF lesion causes inability to look left; the unopposed right PPRF deviates the eyes to the right.

stem: A patient with multiple sclerosis has no horizontal eye movement on attempted rightward gaze. On leftward gaze, the right eye fails to adduct while the left eye abducts normally. The only horizontal movement she retains is abduction of the left eye. Which is the most likely lesion?

options.text: Left dorsal pons involving medial longitudinal fasciculus
Right dorsal pons involving CN VI nucleus/PPRF and MLF
Right rostral midbrain involving CN III and red nucleus
Left cavernous sinus involving abducens and trochlear
Bilateral frontal eye fields in frontal motor cortex

explanation: One-and-a-half syndrome: an ipsilateral abducens nucleus/PPRF lesion (gaze palsy toward that side; the "one") plus ipsilateral MLF (INO on the other direction; the "half"). The only preserved horizontal movement is abduction of the contralateral eye.

stem: A 22-year-old man with a pineal germinoma has headaches from hydrocephalus. He cannot look upward, his pupils react poorly to light but constrict to near effort, and his eyes show convergence-retraction nystagmus. Which is the most likely lesion location?

options.text: Ventral caudal pons involving corticospinal fibers
Medullary pyramids and hypoglossal nerve rootlets
Dorsal rostral midbrain pretectum and commissure
Frontal eye fields within middle frontal gyri
Occipital striate visual cortex bordering calcarine

explanation: Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome: pineal tumors compress the dorsal midbrain, causing paralysis of upward gaze, light-near pupillary dissociation, convergence-retraction nystagmus, and eyelid retraction; the tumor may also obstruct the aqueduct, causing hydrocephalus.

stem: A dorsal midbrain tumor destroys the superior colliculi. The patient has normal visual acuity but no longer shifts gaze automatically toward a sudden peripheral flash. Which function of the superior colliculus is impaired?

options.text: Pupillary light reflex to direct illumination
Reflex orienting of eyes and head toward visual cues
Near triad accommodation and pupillary miosis
Sound localization and auditory spatial mapping
Sympathetic pupillary dilation in darkness

explanation: The superior colliculus mediates reflexive saccades and head/eye orienting toward visual stimuli (via tectospinal pathways). The pretectal area mediates pupillary reflexes; the inferior colliculus orients to sound.

stem: A 24-year-old has a focal seizure in which her eyes and head turn forcefully to the left. EEG shows epileptiform discharges over the right frontal convexity. Which structure is the likely seizure focus?

options.text: Left frontal eye field
Right frontal eye field
Right PPRF
Left PPRF
Right occipital lobe

explanation: A seizure focus in the right FEF drives the eyes and head to the left (away from the focus). A stroke would produce the opposite (deviation toward the lesion).

stem: A 26-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has failure of adduction of both eyes on lateral gaze with abducting nystagmus; convergence is intact. Which is the most likely lesion?

options.text: Bilateral abducens palsies
Bilateral frontal eye field lesions
Bilateral MLF demyelination
Bilateral oculomotor nerve palsies
Bilateral PPRF lesions

explanation: Bilateral INO in a young adult suggests MS (bilateral MLF demyelination); unilateral INO in an older adult more likely reflects brainstem infarction. Convergence is preserved because it bypasses the MLF.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with an aneurysm of the intracavernous internal carotid artery first notices horizontal double vision. Which nerve is typically affected first?

options.text: CN III
CN IV
CN VI
V1
V2

explanation: CN VI lies free in the sinus lateral to the internal carotid artery, whereas CN III, IV, V1, and V2 run in the lateral wall; an aneurysm of the intracavernous ICA therefore affects CN VI first.

stem: A patient with a cavernous sinus tumor has diplopia and loss of sensation over the forehead and cheek, but chewing strength and jaw sensation are normal. Which nerve does NOT pass through the cavernous sinus?

options.text: Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
Maxillary nerve (V2)
Mandibular nerve (V3)
Abducens nerve (CN VI)

explanation: CN V3 (mandibular) exits through foramen ovale and does not enter the cavernous sinus. CN III, IV, V1, V2, and VI pass through it, along with the ICA and sympathetic fibers.

stem: A 19-year-old squeezes a pimple near the nasolabial fold and days later develops fever, periorbital edema, and ophthalmoplegia. Through which route did the infection most likely spread?

options.text: Facial vein to superior ophthalmic vein to cavernous sinus
Facial artery to internal carotid artery to cavernous sinus
Facial lymphatic drainage into deep cervical lymph nodes
Retromandibular vein to external jugular to sigmoid sinus
Direct retrograde bacterial transit via arachnoid spaces

explanation: The 'danger triangle' of the face drains via the facial vein to the superior ophthalmic vein (valveless veins), which empties into the cavernous sinus; infection can spread retrograde to cause septic cavernous sinus thrombosis.

stem: To test the integrity of CN IV in the right eye, the examiner asks the patient to do which of the following?

options.text: Look laterally
Look medially, then up
Look laterally, then down
Look medially, then down
Converge on a near target

explanation: With the eye adducted, the superior oblique (CN IV) depresses it and the inferior oblique (CN III) elevates it; when abducted, the superior and inferior recti do these jobs. So 'look medially then down' tests CN IV.

stem: What is the resting eye position in a complete right CN III palsy?

options.text: Eye deviated up and in from superior rectus action
Eye deviated down and in from inferior rectus action
Eye deviated down and out from superior oblique and CN VI
Eye maintained in central position without strabismus
Eye deviated up and out from inferior oblique action

explanation: In complete CN III palsy, only the lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) function, producing a 'down and out' eye with ptosis and a dilated pupil.

stem: Why is the ptosis in Horner syndrome mild whereas it is severe in CN III palsy?

options.text: Horner syndrome paralyzes only the levator palpebrae superioris muscle
Horner syndrome selectively impairs orbicularis oculi eyelid closure
Horner syndrome disrupts third cranial nerve somatic motor output
Horner syndrome spares both the superior tarsal and levator muscles
Horner syndrome paralyzes superior tarsal muscle while levator remains intact

explanation: In Horner syndrome, sympathetic denervation of the superior tarsal (Mueller) muscle produces mild ptosis. The levator palpebrae (CN III) is intact. CN III palsy paralyzes the levator and causes severe ptosis.

stem: An ophthalmologist uses 2.5% phenylephrine drops for a dilated exam in a patient in whom cycloplegia is undesirable. Which mechanism explains the pupillary dilation?

options.text: Muscarinic M3 receptor antagonism producing passive pupillary dilation
Alpha-1 adrenergic agonism producing active pupillary dilator contraction
Beta-2 adrenergic receptor agonism promoting ciliary muscle relaxation
Muscarinic M3 receptor agonism producing active pupillary constriction
Inhibition of presynaptic norepinephrine reuptake in the ciliary body

explanation: Phenylephrine is an alpha-1 agonist that contracts the radial dilator pupillae, dilating the pupil without cycloplegia. Anticholinergics (atropine, tropicamide) block M3 receptors, causing mydriasis and cycloplegia.

stem: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus travel in CN III to the ciliary ganglion. Which receptor mediates transmission onto the postganglionic neurons?

options.text: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
Muscarinic acetylcholine receptor
Alpha-1 adrenergic receptor
Beta-1 adrenergic receptor
Dopamine receptor

explanation:
Parasympathetic ganglia use nicotinic receptors on postganglionic neurons; the postganglionic neurons then release acetylcholine onto M3 muscarinic receptors on the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle.


---

stem: A 63-year-old hyperopic woman develops sudden severe left eye pain, headache, nausea, and blurred vision with halos around lights shortly after entering a dark movie theater. Examination shows a red eye with a mid-dilated, minimally reactive pupil and a hazy cornea; the globe feels firm. Which best explains her acute attack?

options.text: Hypersecretion of aqueous humor by the ciliary body epithelium
Pupillary dilation with peripheral iris occlusion of the angle
Neovascularization of the anterior chamber angle from ischemia
Posterior vitreous traction inducing a neurosensory tear
Fluid accumulation between Bruch membrane and pigment layer

explanation: Acute angle-closure glaucoma, classically in middle-aged hyperopic patients. Pupillary dilation (dim light, anticholinergics) bunches the peripheral iris against the trabecular meshwork and blocks aqueous drainage, causing a sudden IOP rise (red, painful, rock-hard eye, halos, nausea). Glaucoma is a drainage problem, not overproduction. Pilocarpine causes miosis, pulling the iris from the angle.

stem: A 66-year-old Black man is diagnosed with primary open-angle glaucoma with an IOP of 28 mm Hg. He is started on a once-nightly eye drop. At follow-up, his IOP has improved, but he notes his eyelashes have become longer and thicker. This drug lowers IOP primarily by which mechanism?

options.text: Decreasing aqueous humor production by blocking beta receptors on the ciliary epithelium
Decreasing aqueous humor production by stimulating alpha-2 receptors
Increasing uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humor
Constricting the pupil to widen the iridocorneal angle
Inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body

explanation: Prostaglandin F2-alpha analogs (latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost) increase uveoscleral outflow and are first-line for open-angle glaucoma. Adverse effects: eyelash growth, iris darkening, periocular pigmentation. Beta-blockers, alpha agonists, and CAIs decrease production; cholinomimetics cause miosis and increase outflow.

stem: A 59-year-old man with primary open-angle glaucoma also has moderate persistent asthma. Which topical ocular medication should be avoided?

options.text: Latanoprost
Timolol
Brimonidine
Dorzolamide
Travoprost

explanation: Timolol, a nonselective beta-blocker, lowers IOP by decreasing aqueous production but is systemically absorbed and can cause bronchospasm and bradycardia, so it is avoided in asthma/COPD. The other agents are not contraindicated in asthma.

stem: A 62-year-old highly myopic man reports 2 days of new floaters and flashes of light in the right eye, followed this morning by a painless, curtain-like shadow progressing across his vision. Which best explains his vision loss?

options.text: Separation of neurosensory retina from pigment epithelium
Impaired trabecular meshwork aqueous outflow with high IOP
Accumulation of extracellular drusen beneath the epithelium
Apoptotic loss of rod photoreceptors with peripheral pigment
Insoluble cross-linking and aggregation of lens crystallins

explanation: In retinal detachment the neurosensory retina separates from the RPE/choroid. The outer retina (photoreceptors) depends on the choroid for blood supply and on the RPE for metabolic support, so photoreceptors die without prompt reattachment. Posterior vitreous detachment and retinal tears (floaters, flashes) commonly precede it. Treatment: laser for early tears, surgery for advanced/macula-involving detachment.

stem: A healthy 3-month-old infant is found at a well-child visit to have an absent red reflex in the left eye, and a dense white lens opacity is confirmed. The right eye is normal. Which is the main reason prompt surgical removal is critical in this infant, compared with a similar finding in an elderly adult?

options.text: Surgical delay causing contiguous spread into the contralateral lens
Rapid progression of lens tumescence producing acute closed glaucoma
Ischemic degeneration of perifoveal photoreceptors within few days
Cortical visual deprivation during development causing amblyopia
Chronic mechanical vitreous traction predisposing to retinal tear

explanation: Visual cortical circuits develop in the first year of life and require balanced, focused input from both eyes. A dense unilateral congenital cataract causes unequal input, leading to amblyopia and permanent deficits unless removed promptly. Adult cataracts are slowly progressive and treated electively.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with known drusen in both eyes reports that over the past week straight lines such as door frames look wavy and a central blurry spot has appeared in the right eye. Fundoscopy shows subretinal hemorrhage at the macula. Which is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral antioxidant vitamin and zinc supplementation
Panretinal laser photocoagulation
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injection
Topical timolol
Cataract extraction

explanation: Metamorphopsia, central scotoma, and subretinal hemorrhage in a patient with drusen indicate conversion from dry to wet (neovascular) AMD: choroidal neovascularization between Bruch membrane and the RPE. Treatment: intravitreal anti-VEGF. Antioxidant/zinc supplements slow dry AMD only; panretinal photocoagulation is for proliferative diabetic retinopathy.

stem: A 38-year-old man with type 1 diabetes for 18 years and poor glycemic control reports gradually blurred vision. Dilated fundus examination shows microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and fragile new vessels at the optic disc. Which best explains the new vessel growth, and what is an appropriate treatment?

options.text: Excess aqueous humor secretion; topical beta-blocker
Autoantibodies against retinal antigens; systemic corticosteroids
Rhodopsin gene mutation; oral vitamin A
Drusen deposition; antioxidant vitamins
Retinal ischemia-induced VEGF release; laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF therapy

explanation: Hyperglycemia damages retinal capillaries (microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, edema), causing ischemia. Hypoxic retina releases VEGF, driving neovascularization (proliferative DR); fragile vessels bleed and cause traction. Treatment: glycemic control, panretinal laser, intravitreal anti-VEGF. ROP has the same VEGF-driven mechanism.

stem: A 22-year-old man who sleeps in his extended-wear contact lenses presents with 1 day of severe right eye pain, photophobia, tearing, and decreased vision. Examination shows conjunctival injection and a white corneal infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect that takes up fluorescein. There is no hypopyon. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hordeolum
Bacterial conjunctivitis
Anterior uveitis
Bacterial keratitis
Blepharitis

explanation: Contact lens overuse (especially sleeping in lenses) predisposes to bacterial keratitis, classically Pseudomonas aeruginosa: pain, photophobia, tearing, corneal infiltrate/ulcer staining with fluorescein. Bacterial conjunctivitis has purulent discharge with a clear cornea; anterior uveitis shows anterior chamber cells and ciliary flush without corneal infiltrate; hordeolum is a painful lid gland infection; blepharitis is lid margin scaling.

stem: A newborn has a unilateral small, structurally disorganized right eye with poor vision. Which is an essential part of long-term management?

options.text: Observation only
Patching the normal eye to prevent amblyopia
Topical timolol
Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections
Prophylactic enucleation

explanation: Unilateral microphthalmos invariably causes amblyopia because the cortex receives unequal input during the critical period. Patching of the better eye is required, along with monitoring for cataract, glaucoma, and retinal detachment.

stem: A child has had a keyhole-shaped pupil since birth. Which is the embryologic basis of this finding?

options.text: Failure of the optic fissure to close
Persistence of the pupillary membrane
Defective neural crest migration to the trabecular meshwork
Hyperoxia-induced retinal vessel obliteration
Limbal stem cell failure

explanation: Coloboma results from failure of the optic (choroidal) fissure to close, classically producing an inferonasal keyhole iris defect, sometimes involving lens, choroid, retina, or optic disc.

stem: A 4-year-old with sporadic aniridia, nystagmus, and developmental delay has a deletion at chromosome 11p13. Which tumor is this child most at risk for?

options.text: Neuroblastoma
Hepatoblastoma
Retinoblastoma
Wilms tumor
Medulloblastoma

explanation: Sporadic aniridia (PAX6, 11p13) can be part of WAGR syndrome: 11p13 deletion including adjacent WT1. Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary anomalies, Retardation. Serial abdominal ultrasound screening for Wilms tumor is indicated.

stem: A 6-month-old has excessive tearing, photophobia, and eyelid squeezing, with enlarged, hazy corneas bilaterally. IOP is elevated. Which is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Topical antibiotics
Patching therapy
Urgent goniotomy or trabeculotomy
Oral vitamin A
Observation until age 5

explanation: Congenital glaucoma (trabecular meshwork malformation): tearing, photophobia, blepharospasm, and enlarged hazy corneas (buphthalmos) because the infant eye distends. Blinding if untreated; goniotomy or trabeculotomy bypasses outflow resistance.

stem: A 28-week, 900-g infant who required prolonged supplemental oxygen is found at screening to have an abnormal ridge of vessels at the border of vascular and avascular peripheral retina. Which best explains the pathogenesis?

options.text: Autoimmune antibody destruction targeting capillary basement membrane
Excessive ciliary body aqueous production causing ocular hypertension
Premature denaturation and aggregation of cytoplasmic alpha-crystallins
Failure of physiological apoptosis and regression of hyaloid vessels
Hyperoxia vessel arrest followed by hypoxia-driven VEGF proliferation

explanation: ROP arises in the most premature infants. Hyperoxia and loss of placental growth factors suppress VEGF and halt vessel growth; as the avascular retina becomes hypoxic, VEGF surges, causing abnormal neovascularization at the vascular/avascular border. Treatment: laser or anti-VEGF. Screening: under 31 weeks and 1500 g.

stem: A 2-year-old has a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria) in the left eye and an absent red reflex. A calcified retinal mass is seen on ultrasound. Loss of function of which gene is responsible?

options.text: RB1
TP53
WT1
NF1
PAX6

explanation: Retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood, presents with leukocoria. Caused by biallelic loss of the RB1 tumor suppressor (13q14), which restrains the G1-S transition. Hereditary cases carry osteosarcoma risk.

stem: A 65-year-old Black man is incidentally found to have IOP of 26 mm Hg and enlarged optic disc cups. He has no eye symptoms. If untreated, which clinical course is expected?

options.text: Painless peripheral visual field loss with optic disc cupping
Severe ocular pain, conjunctival injection, and rainbow halos
Progressive central scotoma with distortion on the Amsler grid
Sudden onset of flashes, multiple dark floaters, and a curtain
Bilateral visual blur with nighttime headlight glare and haze

explanation: POAG is a progressive optic neuropathy with disc cupping, usually with elevated IOP, causing painless gradual peripheral field loss; central vision is preserved until late, so patients are asymptomatic. More common and severe in Black patients; requires screening.

stem: Which sequence correctly describes the normal path of aqueous humor flow?

options.text: Choroid, vitreous, retina, canal of Schlemm
Ciliary body, anterior chamber, pupil, posterior chamber, trabecular meshwork
Ciliary body, posterior chamber, pupil, anterior chamber, trabecular meshwork, canal of Schlemm
Lens, anterior chamber, canal of Schlemm, trabecular meshwork
Retina, vitreous chamber, trabecular meshwork

explanation: Aqueous humor is made by the ciliary body, flows into the posterior chamber, through the pupil into the anterior chamber, then drains via the trabecular meshwork into the canal of Schlemm. Blockage at the pupil (pupillary block) or at the angle raises IOP.

stem: A patient with glaucoma begins brimonidine drops. Which is the primary mechanism by which this drug lowers IOP?

options.text: Increases trabecular outflow by ciliary muscle contraction
Decreases aqueous humor production by alpha-2 stimulation
Increases uveoscleral outflow by prostaglandin receptor activation
Blocks carbonic anhydrase
Blocks beta-2 receptors on ciliary epithelium

explanation: Brimonidine and apraclonidine are alpha-2 agonists that reduce aqueous production (and increase uveoscleral outflow). Adverse effects: ocular allergy/pruritus, blurry vision; brimonidine should be avoided in infants (CNS depression).

stem: A patient receiving oral acetazolamide for acute angle-closure glaucoma reports tingling in the fingers and is found to have a low serum bicarbonate. Which adverse effect is most likely?

options.text: Reversible hypertrichosis with eyelash lengthening
Sinus bradycardia and acute reactive bronchospasm
Heterochromia with hyperpigmentation of the iris
Non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with paresthesias
Accommodative ciliary spasm with periorbital aches

explanation: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, dorzolamide) reduce bicarbonate and aqueous production. Systemic acetazolamide causes paresthesias, non-anion-gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, and kidney stones; avoid in sulfonamide allergy.

stem: A patient with acute angle-closure glaucoma is given topical pilocarpine. Which ocular effects are expected?

options.text: Pupillary mydriasis with cycloplegic loss of near focus
Progressive hyperpigmentation of the iris and lashes
Enhanced uveoscleral outflow without ciliary alteration
Transient systemic hypotension with compensatory tachycardia
Pupillary miosis with dim-light blur and ciliary spasm

explanation: Pilocarpine contracts the ciliary muscle (opening the trabecular meshwork) and constricts the pupil (pulling the iris away from the angle). Adverse effects: miosis (poor night vision), accommodative spasm (brow ache, induced myopia), systemic cholinergic effects.

stem: A 60-year-old hyperopic woman with a shallow anterior chamber develops an acute painful red eye after receiving a scopolamine patch for motion sickness. Which drug class is responsible for precipitating the attack?

options.text: Parasympathomimetic miotics like pilocarpine
Anticholinergic mydriatics like scopolamine
Beta-adrenergic antagonists like timolol
Prostaglandin F2-alpha analogues like latanoprost
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors like acetazolamide

explanation: Anticholinergics (atropine, scopolamine, tropicamide, some antihistamines and tricyclics) cause mydriasis, which can bunch the iris against the angle in narrow-angle eyes, precipitating acute angle-closure. Cholinomimetics treat it.

stem: A 72-year-old man notes that he can briefly read without his reading glasses, but his distance vision has gradually worsened with glare while driving at night. Slit-lamp exam shows nuclear lens opacification. Which refractive change underlies his transient improvement in near vision?

options.text: Hyperopic shift
Astigmatism
Myopic shift
Complete loss of accommodation only
Peripheral field constriction

explanation: Nuclear sclerosis increases the lens nucleus refractive index, producing a myopic shift ("second sight"), along with progressive blur and glare. Cataract is age-related clouding from denatured, accumulated lens proteins.

stem: A neonate has poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, and bilateral cataracts after beginning breast milk. Accumulation of which compound within the lens most directly causes the cataracts?

options.text: Galactitol
Fructose-1-phosphate
Homogentisic acid
Glycogen
Phenylpyruvate

explanation: Classic galactosemia (galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency): jaundice, hepatomegaly, vomiting after milk, E coli sepsis risk, bilateral cataracts. Lens aldose reductase converts galactose to galactitol, which accumulates osmotically and opacifies the lens. Diabetic cataracts involve sorbitol.

stem: A 75-year-old woman has progressive visual blur and glare that prevent her from driving. Slit-lamp exam shows a dense nuclear cataract. Which is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Topical non-selective beta-blockers like timolol
Intravitreal anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody injections
Argon laser panretinal scatter photocoagulation
Phacoemulsification with intraocular lens replacement
Topical parasympathomimetic miotics like pilocarpine

explanation: Symptomatic cataracts are treated with phacoemulsification and IOL implantation, the most common surgery worldwide, with a very high success rate. No medication reverses the opacity; infants require urgent surgery.

stem: A 79-year-old woman has gradually worsening central blur. Fundoscopy of the macula shows multiple yellow deposits. Which finding is the hallmark of her condition?

options.text: Proliferative neovascularization across the optic nerve disc
Extracellular drusen beneath the retinal pigment epithelium
Perivascular bone-spicule pigment deposits in the periphery
Marked retinal pallor with a prominent cherry-red foveal spot
Diffuse cotton-wool spots and flame-shaped microhemorrhages

explanation: Drusen (yellow extracellular deposits between Bruch membrane and the RPE) mark dry (atrophic) AMD, the most common form. Slow central vision loss; antioxidant/zinc supplements slow progression. It can convert to wet AMD.

stem: Counseling for a patient with early age-related macular degeneration should emphasize modifying which risk factor?

options.text: Hypercalcemia
Myopia
Cigarette smoking
Hypothyroidism
Oral contraceptives

explanation: Age is the strongest AMD risk factor, but the main modifiable risk factor is cigarette smoking. Central vision is lost (reading, driving, faces) with metamorphopsia; peripheral vision is spared.

stem: A 45-year-old man with long-standing proliferative diabetic retinopathy develops a retinal detachment. Fibrovascular bands are seen pulling the retina away from the pigment epithelium. Which type of detachment is this?

options.text: Rhegmatogenous
Tractional
Exudative
Choroidal melanoma
Pigmentary

explanation: Tractional detachment: fibrovascular proliferation (e.g., PDR) pulls the retina off the RPE. Rhegmatogenous follows a retinal tear (often after posterior vitreous detachment); exudative follows subretinal fluid accumulation.

stem: A 16-year-old has difficulty seeing at night and has noticed his peripheral vision narrowing. His uncle has a similar problem. Fundoscopy shows bone-spicule pigmentation in the periphery and ERG is markedly reduced. Which cells degenerate first?

options.text: Cones first, then rods
Retinal ganglion cells
Bipolar cells
Retinal pigment epithelium only
Rod photoreceptors first, then cones

explanation: Retinitis pigmentosa: genetic rod-cone dystrophy. Rods degenerate first (night blindness, then peripheral field loss/tunnel vision), with bone-spicule pigment, waxy disc pallor, arteriolar attenuation, and reduced or extinguished ERG.

stem: A 45-year-old man with blood pressure 240/140 mm Hg has headache and blurred vision. Fundoscopy shows arteriolar narrowing, flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and optic disc swelling. Which diagnosis is indicated?

options.text: Hypertensive emergency with accelerated retinopathy
Primary open-angle glaucoma with optic disc cupping
Diabetic macular edema with microvascular exudates
Central retinal artery occlusion with foveal pallor
Demyelinating optic neuritis with papillar swelling

explanation: Papilledema with flame hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, and arteriolar changes with severely elevated BP signifies malignant (accelerated) hypertension, a hypertensive emergency. Chronic hypertension causes arteriolar narrowing and AV nicking.

stem: A 68-year-old man with atherosclerosis has sudden painless loss of vision in the right eye. Fundoscopy shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula. What is the most likely source?

options.text: Retinal vein thrombosis with extensive hemorrhages
Vitreous hemorrhage from neovascular vessel rupture
Autoimmune demyelinating optic neuritis episodes
Carotid atheroembolus occluding the retinal artery
Pupillary block with acute closed angle glaucoma

explanation: Central retinal artery occlusion: sudden painless monocular vision loss with a pale, edematous retina and a cherry-red spot at the fovea (thin foveal retina reveals the choroid, which has a separate blood supply). Usual source: embolus from the ipsilateral carotid or heart.

stem: A 66-year-old man with hypertension has sudden painless blurring of vision in one eye. Fundoscopy shows diffuse flame hemorrhages in all quadrants, dilated tortuous veins, and optic disc swelling. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Central retinal artery occlusion
Central retinal vein occlusion
Retinal detachment
Dry age-related macular degeneration
Retinitis pigmentosa

explanation: CRVO: painless vision loss with diffuse retinal hemorrhages ("blood and thunder"), dilated tortuous veins, disc edema. Risks: hypertension, diabetes, hypercoagulability. Ischemia drives VEGF release, risking neovascularization and neovascular glaucoma.

stem: A 28-year-old woman has a firm, painless, rubbery nodule in the right upper eyelid that has enlarged slowly over 3 weeks. There is no erythema or tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hordeolum
Blepharitis
Preseptal cellulitis
Dacryocystitis
Chalazion

explanation: Chalazion: painless, firm, rubbery eyelid nodule from meibomian/Zeis gland obstruction with sterile lipogranulomatous inflammation; warm compresses help. Hordeolum (stye) is acute, painful, red, usually S aureus.

stem: A 22-year-old has a red, watery, irritated right eye after 3 days of sore throat. Examination shows follicles on the inferior conjunctiva and a tender preauricular lymph node. The cornea is clear. Which agent is most likely?

options.text: Adenovirus
Staphylococcus aureus
Haemophilus influenzae
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
An airborne allergen

explanation: Adenoviral conjunctivitis: watery discharge, follicular reaction, tender preauricular lymphadenopathy, recent URI/pharyngitis; highly contagious and self-limited. Bacterial conjunctivitis: purulent discharge; allergic: itching with papillae.

stem: A 3-day-old neonate born to a mother who received no prenatal care has bilateral swollen eyelids with profuse purulent discharge. Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci. Which organism is responsible?

options.text: Chemical irritation
Chlamydia trachomatis
Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Herpes simplex virus
Staphylococcus epidermidis

explanation: Neonatal conjunctivitis timing: chemical (silver nitrate) within 24 h; Neisseria gonorrhoeae at about days 2-5 with profuse purulent discharge (gram-negative diplococci; can perforate cornea); Chlamydia trachomatis days 5-14 with mucopurulent discharge. Gonococcal disease needs systemic ceftriaxone.

stem: A 28-year-old man with chronic low back pain and morning stiffness has a painful, photophobic red eye with ciliary flush and cells in the anterior chamber. The pupil is small and irregular. Which is the most appropriate topical therapy?

options.text: Topical broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibiotic drops
Topical parasympathomimetic miotics such as pilocarpine
Topical dual-action mast cell stabilizer antihistamines
Topical corticosteroids and cycloplegic-mydriatic agents
Intravitreal vascular endothelial growth factor blockers

explanation: Anterior uveitis (iritis): pain, photophobia, limbal redness (ciliary flush), cells and flare or hypopyon, small irregular pupil from synechiae. Associated with HLA-B27 diseases (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis), sarcoidosis, JIA. Treatment: topical steroids plus a cycloplegic/mydriatic to relieve pain and prevent synechiae.

stem: A 35-year-old with a painful red eye, photophobia, and decreased corneal sensation has a branching linear ulcer on the cornea that takes up fluorescein. Which is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Topical corticosteroids alone
Topical or oral antiviral therapy
Topical pilocarpine
Topical antihistamines
Intravitreal anti-VEGF

explanation: A branching dendritic ulcer staining with fluorescein is characteristic of HSV keratitis, which also reduces corneal sensation. Treatment: topical or oral antiviral (acyclovir, ganciclovir); topical steroids alone can worsen epithelial disease.

stem: A 7-year-old with fever, sinusitis, and a swollen red eyelid is being evaluated. Which finding most strongly indicates orbital rather than preseptal cellulitis?

options.text: Superficial erythema localized across the eyelid
Mild edema confined anterior to the orbital septum
High-grade fever with systemic peripheral malaise
Recent upper respiratory tract bacterial sinusitis
Proptosis with painful, restricted ocular movements

explanation:
Preseptal cellulitis involves eyelid tissue anterior to the orbital septum and spares eye movements and vision. Orbital cellulitis (usually from ethmoid sinusitis): fever, proptosis, painful or limited extraocular movements, possible vision loss; needs contrast CT and IV antibiotics (risk of abscess and cavernous sinus thrombosis).


---

stem: A 54-year-old woman reports brief episodes of intense spinning vertigo each time she rolls onto her right side in bed or tilts her head back to reach a high shelf. Each episode lasts about 30 seconds and is accompanied by nausea. She has no tinnitus, hearing loss, or focal neurologic deficits. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver with the head turned to the right reproduces her symptoms with torsional nystagmus. Which of the following best explains the underlying mechanism?

options.text: Excess endolymph accumulating within the cochlear and vestibular spaces
Calcium carbonate crystals displaced from the otolithic membrane into a canal
Schwann cell tumor expanding along the acoustic and vestibular branches
Post-viral inflammation of the membranous labyrinth and vestibular nerve
Ischemic infarction of the vestibular nuclei in the dorsolateral brainstem

explanation: BPPV: otoconia detach from the utricular macula's otolithic membrane and drift into a semicircular canal, abnormally stimulating the cupula with head position change. Episodes are brief (<1 min), positional, and without hearing loss; the Epley maneuver relocates the crystals. (A) Meniere; (C) schwannoma; (D) labyrinthitis (persistent, days); (E) central vertigo with other brainstem signs.

stem: A 46-year-old man has had four episodes over 3 months of severe spinning vertigo lasting about 1 hour each, with nausea, a sensation of fullness in the left ear, and a roaring tinnitus in the left ear. Between attacks he notes his hearing on the left is worse than before. A 512-Hz tuning fork placed on the forehead is heard louder in the right ear; Rinne testing shows air > bone conduction in both ears. Which of the following is the most likely underlying pathophysiology?

options.text: Displaced otoconia in the posterior semicircular canal
Schwann cell tumor of the vestibular nerve
Excess endolymph in the endolymphatic space producing increased pressure
Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve and labyrinth
Eustachian tube dysfunction with middle ear effusion

explanation: Episodic vertigo (minutes to hours) with aural fullness, tinnitus, and fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss is Meniere disease (endolymphatic hydrops). Weber to the good (right) ear with normal Rinne = left sensorineural loss. Treatment: sodium restriction and diuretics. BPPV is brief without hearing loss; schwannoma is progressive; labyrinthitis is continuous for days; middle ear disease causes conductive loss.

stem: A 33-year-old woman reports 2 years of progressive right-sided hearing loss that worsened during her recent pregnancy. Otoscopy shows normal tympanic membranes bilaterally. A 512-Hz tuning fork on the midline forehead is heard louder in the right ear. On the right, the tuning fork is heard louder when held against the mastoid than when held next to the ear canal; on the left, the reverse is true. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Right sensorineural hearing loss due to cochlear hair cell loss
Left sensorineural hearing loss due to ototoxic drug exposure
Right vestibular schwannoma
Right conductive hearing loss due to stapes fixation
Bilateral presbycusis

explanation: Weber lateralizes to the affected ear in conductive loss and to the good ear in sensorineural loss. Rinne is abnormal (bone > air) on the right, confirming right conductive loss. Normal TM, young woman, worsening in pregnancy = otosclerosis (stapes footplate fixation).

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with 1 year of progressive right-sided hearing loss, constant ringing in the right ear, and unsteadiness when walking. Over the past 2 months he has noticed numbness of the right cheek. Examination shows a diminished right corneal reflex and mild right facial weakness. Weber lateralizes to the left, and Rinne shows air > bone bilaterally. MRI reveals an enhancing right cerebellopontine angle mass. Which of the following best explains his facial numbness and weakness?

options.text: Direct infiltrative invasion of the primary dorsal cochlear nucleus
Compression of CN V and CN VII at the cerebellopontine angle by tumor
Compression of CN IX and CN X at the posterior jugular foramen region
Involvement of ophthalmic and maxillary branches within cavernous sinus
Ischemic infarction of the lateral medullary tegmentum and tractus

explanation: A vestibular schwannoma (Schwann cell tumor of CN VIII) causes unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance. As it enlarges in the cerebellopontine angle it compresses CN VII (facial weakness) and CN V (decreased facial sensation and corneal reflex). Treatment: surgery or gamma knife.

stem: A 60-year-old man has a small hemorrhage in the right dorsal pons. He complains of difficulty determining where sounds are coming from, but pure-tone audiometry shows normal thresholds in both ears. Which of the following structures is most likely damaged?

options.text: Right cochlear division of CN VIII
Right cochlear nucleus
Right spiral ganglion
Right lateral lemniscus
Right organ of Corti

explanation: Auditory input becomes bilateral above the superior olivary nuclei (via the trapezoid body). Lesions at the lateral lemniscus or above cause little hearing loss but impair sound localization, which depends on comparing input from both ears. Lesions of the organ of Corti, spiral ganglion, CN VIII, or cochlear nucleus cause ipsilateral deafness.
