stem: A 67-year-old man with an infarct involving the lateral vestibular nucleus has normal strength on manual muscle testing but is unable to maintain an upright posture and falls when standing without support. Loss of which of the following pathways most directly explains his symptoms?

options.text: Medial vestibulospinal tract
Lateral corticospinal tract
Lateral vestibulospinal tract
Rubrospinal tract
Medial longitudinal fasciculus

explanation: The lateral vestibular nucleus gives rise to the uncrossed lateral vestibulospinal tract, which drives antigravity extensors for upright posture and balance. The medial vestibulospinal tract controls neck muscles to keep the head upright; the MLF carries vestibulo-ocular fibers to CN III, IV, VI nuclei.

stem: A 71-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes, and atrial fibrillation develops sudden vertigo, nausea, and gait instability. He also has dysarthria, left facial numbness, and diplopia. Hearing is intact. Horizontal nystagmus is present. Which finding best supports a central rather than a peripheral cause of vertigo?

options.text: Nystagmus that does not diminish with visual fixation
Vertigo that fatigues with repeated provocation
Prominent tinnitus
Unilateral hearing loss
Intense vertigo with severe nausea

explanation: Peripheral vertigo: intense, fatigable, nystagmus suppressed by visual fixation, hearing loss/tinnitus possible. Central vertigo (brainstem or cerebellar infarct): milder, non-fatigable, nystagmus NOT suppressed by fixation, with other sensory, motor, or cerebellar findings and no hearing loss.

stem: A 66-year-old man with chronic kidney disease is treated for sepsis with 10 days of intravenous gentamicin and furosemide. He develops bilateral tinnitus and has difficulty hearing high-pitched voices. Weber is midline and Rinne shows air > bone bilaterally. Which of the following best describes the likely site of injury and audiometric pattern?

options.text: Hair cells at the apex of the cochlea; low-frequency sensorineural loss
Stapes footplate fixation; conductive loss
Compression of CN VIII at the cerebellopontine angle; unilateral loss
Superior olivary nuclei; impaired sound localization
Hair cells at the base of the cochlea; high-frequency sensorineural loss

explanation: Aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, cisplatin, and salicylates are ototoxic and damage cochlear hair cells, typically starting at the base (high frequencies; stiff, narrow basilar membrane). Result: bilateral sensorineural loss with normal Rinne and midline Weber. Same basal hair cell loss underlies presbycusis.

stem: A 29-year-old woman wakes with drooping of the entire right side of her face, including the forehead, and is unable to close her right eye. She also reports that everyday sounds seem unusually loud in her right ear. Dysfunction of which muscle best explains the abnormal sound sensitivity?

options.text: Tensor tympani, innervated by CN V
Stapedius, innervated by CN VII
Medial pterygoid, innervated by CN V
Tensor veli palatini, innervated by CN V
Levator veli palatini, innervated by CN X

explanation: This is Bell palsy (LMN CN VII lesion). The stapedius (CN VII) dampens stapes movement in response to loud noise; paralysis causes hyperacusis. The tensor tympani (CN V3) is unaffected.

stem: A researcher records from cochlear inner hair cells in vitro. When the stereocilia are deflected toward the tallest stereocilia (kinocilium side), the cell depolarizes. Which ion movement is primarily responsible?

options.text: Na+ influx from perilymph
Ca2+ efflux into endolymph
K+ influx from the K+-rich endolymph
Cl- influx from perilymph
K+ efflux into perilymph

explanation: Endolymph (scala media) is high K+, low Na+. Stereocilia deflection opens mechanically gated channels at their tips; K+ enters down its gradient, depolarizing the cell; Ca2+ then enters through voltage-gated channels and glutamate is released onto spiral ganglion neurons.

stem: Which of the following structures secretes the K+-rich endolymph that bathes the stereocilia of cochlear hair cells?

options.text: Choroid plexus
Stria vascularis
Spiral ganglion
Tectorial membrane
Ciliary body

explanation: The stria vascularis, a vascular epithelium in the lateral wall of the scala media, secretes endolymph. Excess endolymph underlies Meniere disease. The choroid plexus makes CSF; the ciliary body makes aqueous humor.

stem: Different sound frequencies maximally displace different regions of the basilar membrane. Which property explains why the base of the cochlea responds best to high frequencies?

options.text: The base of the membrane is narrow and stiff, whereas the apex is wide and flexible
The base contains outer hair cells only, whereas the apex contains inner hair cells
The base is located near the helicotrema, whereas the apex borders the oval window
The base receives facial nerve fibers, whereas the apex receives cochlear branches
The base lacks a tectorial covering, whereas the apex has an anchored membrane

explanation: Tonotopy depends on basilar membrane mechanics: narrow and stiff at the base (oval window) for high frequencies; wide and floppy at the apex (helicotrema) for low frequencies. This is why basal hair cell loss produces high-frequency loss.

stem: Bending of cochlear hair cell stereocilia AWAY from the kinocilium most directly causes which of the following?

options.text: Depolarization and increased neurotransmitter release from the hair cell
Hyperpolarization and decreased firing of the afferent neuron at rest
Calcium influx producing no net alteration in cellular membrane potential
Immediate all-or-none action potential propagation along the stereocilia
Inhibitory GABA release onto postsynaptic spiral ganglion dendrites

explanation: Hair cells fire tonically at baseline. Bending toward the kinocilium depolarizes (firing increases); bending away hyperpolarizes (firing decreases). Hair cells do not generate action potentials themselves.

stem: Which of the following structures contains the cell bodies of the first-order neurons of the auditory pathway, whose axons form the cochlear division of CN VIII?

options.text: Vestibular (Scarpa) ganglion
Cochlear nucleus
Superior olivary nucleus
Spiral ganglion
Inferior colliculus

explanation: Bipolar neurons of the spiral ganglion (in the modiolus) synapse on hair cells and project via the cochlear nerve to the cochlear nuclei at the pontomedullary junction. The vestibular ganglion serves the vestibular division.

stem: A 63-year-old man has an infarct that selectively destroys the right cochlear nuclei at the pontomedullary junction. Which of the following deficits is most likely?

options.text: Deafness in the left ear
Deafness in the right ear
Mild bilateral hearing loss only
Isolated impairment of sound localization
No auditory deficit

explanation: The cochlear nucleus receives ipsilateral input and is the last point where information from one ear travels alone. Destruction causes complete ipsilateral sensorineural deafness. Above this level (superior olive onward) representation is bilateral.

stem: At which of the following levels do second-order auditory axons cross the midline in the trapezoid body to reach the contralateral superior olivary complex and lateral lemniscus?

options.text: Rostral midbrain
Rostral medulla
Thalamus
Caudal pons
Cervical spinal cord

explanation: Second-order axons from the ipsilateral cochlear nucleus travel to the caudal pons; some stay ipsilateral and some cross in the trapezoid body to synapse in the superior olivary nuclei, giving bilateral representation of each ear.

stem: A pineal tumor compresses the dorsal midbrain. The patient's head and eyes no longer turn reflexively toward sudden loud sounds, although audiometry is normal. Which structure's function is most likely impaired?

options.text: Medial geniculate nucleus
Superior olivary nucleus
Inferior colliculus
Cochlear nucleus
Heschl gyrus

explanation: The inferior colliculi (caudal midbrain) are the fourth-order auditory relay and mediate reflex turning of the head and eyes toward sounds (superior colliculi do this for visual stimuli). Fibers then project to the medial geniculate nucleus.

stem: Auditory radiations from the medial geniculate nucleus to the transverse temporal gyrus of Heschl travel through which part of the internal capsule?

options.text: Anterior limb
Genu
Posterior limb
Retrolenticular part
Sublenticular part

explanation: Auditory radiations pass through the sublenticular portion of the internal capsule. The genu carries corticobulbar fibers, the posterior limb corticospinal and sensory fibers, and the retrolenticular part carries optic radiations.

stem: A 66-year-old man has an infarct of the left primary auditory cortex (Heschl gyrus). Pure-tone audiometry is normal in both ears. Which of the following is the most likely deficit?

options.text: Complete sensorineural deafness affecting the left ear
Complete sensorineural deafness affecting the right ear
Total bilateral deafness across all audible frequencies
Impaired sound localization with preserved bilateral hearing
Severe conductive hearing loss with bone-conduction sparing

explanation: Each cochlea projects bilaterally to auditory cortex, so a unilateral cortical (or post-cochlear-nucleus brainstem) lesion is compensated by the opposite hemisphere. Binaural comparison for sound localization is what suffers.

stem: A 3-year-old with a recent upper respiratory infection has ear pain, fever, and a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane. Which of the following sets of organisms most commonly causes this condition?

options.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Aspergillus fumigatus
Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae
Staphylococcus epidermidis and Candida albicans
Neisseria meningitidis and Listeria monocytogenes
Bordetella pertussis and Mycoplasma pneumoniae

explanation: Acute otitis media in young children follows eustachian tube dysfunction after URI; usual pathogens are S pneumoniae, nontypeable H influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Pseudomonas causes otitis externa. Middle ear fluid causes conductive loss.

stem: A 72-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has severe ear pain and purulent drainage for 3 weeks despite topical therapy. Examination shows granulation tissue in the external auditory canal and a new facial nerve palsy. Which organism is the most likely cause?

options.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae
Haemophilus influenzae
Moraxella catarrhalis
Group A Streptococcus
Pseudomonas aeruginosa

explanation: Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa is skull base osteomyelitis from Pseudomonas aeruginosa in diabetic or immunocompromised older patients. Pseudomonas is also the classic cause of simple otitis externa (swimmer's ear).

stem: A 9-year-old with recurrent otitis media has painless, foul-smelling otorrhea and conductive hearing loss. Otoscopy shows a perforated tympanic membrane with a pearly white mass in the middle ear. Which of the following best describes this lesion?

options.text: Keratinizing squamous epithelial cyst that erodes middle ear ossicles
Benign Schwann cell neoplasm expanding along the internal acoustic canal
Sclerotic bony overgrowth producing progressive fixation of the stapes
Endolymphatic hydrops distending the membranous labyrinth compartments
Suppurative bacterial furuncle involving the external cartilaginous canal

explanation: Cholesteatoma is a middle ear cyst of keratinizing squamous epithelium arising from eustachian tube dysfunction or TM perforation/retraction. It enlarges and destroys ossicles, causing conductive hearing loss, and needs surgery.

stem: A 45-year-old factory worker exposed to loud machinery for 20 years has bilateral hearing loss most pronounced around 4000 Hz. Weber is midline and Rinne shows air > bone bilaterally. Which structure is most likely damaged?

options.text: Ossicular chain in the middle ear cavity
Tympanic membrane in the auditory canal
Cochlear hair cells in the organ of Corti
Cranial nerve VIII at the pontine angle
Stapedius muscle within the tympanic wall

explanation: Chronic noise damages hair cells of the organ of Corti, causing bilateral sensorineural loss (normal Rinne, midline Weber), classically with a notch near 4 kHz. Conductive loss arises from external or middle ear disease.

stem: A scuba diver ascends rapidly and has sudden right ear pain and hearing loss. Otoscopy shows a perforated right tympanic membrane. The 512-Hz Weber test is most likely to show which of the following?

options.text: Lateralization to the left ear; Rinne positive bilaterally
Lateralization to the right ear; Rinne negative on the right
Midline Weber sensation; Rinne positive in both ears
Lateralization to the right ear; Rinne positive bilaterally
Lateralization to the left ear; Rinne negative on the left

explanation: Perforation is a conductive defect: Weber lateralizes to the affected (right) ear and bone conduction exceeds air conduction (negative Rinne) on that side. Sensorineural loss shifts Weber to the good ear with preserved air > bone.

stem: A passenger on a rapidly spinning carousel feels a sense of rotation. Which structure transduces angular head acceleration?

options.text: Macula of the utricle in the vestibule
Macula of the saccule in the vestibule
Crista ampullaris of semicircular canals
Organ of Corti in the cochlear duct
Tectorial membrane of the cochlea

explanation: Rotation makes endolymph in the canals lag, deflecting the gelatinous cupula over the crista ampullaris and bending stereocilia. The three canals detect rotation in roll, pitch, and yaw; the maculae detect linear acceleration and gravity.

stem: A passenger standing in an elevator feels the downward acceleration as it begins to descend. Which receptor is most responsible for detecting this vertical linear acceleration?

options.text: Saccular macula
Utricular macula
Anterior semicircular canal
Horizontal semicircular canal
Inner hair cells of the cochlea

explanation: The saccule is oriented vertically and detects vertical linear acceleration and gravity; the utricle is oriented horizontally and detects forward/backward and lateral linear acceleration and head tilt.

stem: Gelatinous membranes are buoyant in endolymph. Which feature of the otolithic membrane allows the maculae to respond to gravity?

options.text: Embedded calcium carbonate crystals that increase membrane density
Extremely high potassium ion concentration within the surrounding fluid
Rigid fibrous attachments directly anchoring to the basilar membrane
Concentric myelin sheaths surrounding the protruding kinocilia shafts
High density of mechanically gated sodium channels across the apex

explanation: Calcium carbonate otoconia add mass so gravity and linear acceleration can displace the membrane relative to the hair cells. Detached otoconia entering a canal cause BPPV.

stem: A healthy subject fixes her gaze on a wall clock while her head is turned briskly to the right. Her eyes move to the left, keeping the clock in focus. Which pathway mediates this reflex?

options.text: Vestibular nuclei to the medial longitudinal fasciculus to the CN III, IV, and VI nuclei
Vestibular nuclei to the lateral vestibulospinal tract to cervical motoneurons
Vestibular nuclei to VPL thalamus to parietotemporal cortex
Superior colliculus to the pretectal area to the Edinger-Westphal nucleus
Frontal eye field to the PPRF to the abducens nucleus

explanation: The vestibulo-ocular reflex sends second-order axons from the vestibular nuclei through the MLF to the oculomotor, trochlear, and abducens nuclei so the eyes counter-rotate during head movement. (C) is the perceptual pathway; (B) is postural control.

stem: Cold water is irrigated into the left external auditory canal of a conscious patient with an intact brainstem. Which of the following is the expected response?

options.text: Nystagmus with fast phase toward the left
Nystagmus with fast phase toward the right
Upbeat vertical nystagmus
Conjugate deviation to the right without nystagmus
No eye movement

explanation: Cold water reduces firing from the irrigated labyrinth, mimicking a lesion on that side: slow phase drifts toward the cooled ear, fast corrective phase beats away. Mnemonic COWS: Cold Opposite, Warm Same (fast-phase direction).

stem: In a comatose patient, rapid rotation of the head to the right causes the eyes to remain fixed in the orbits and move with the head (absent doll's eyes). Which of the following is the best interpretation?

options.text: Normal physiological function of the vestibulo-ocular arc
Dysfunction of the brainstem vestibulo-ocular reflex pathway
Bilateral hemispheric frontal lobe metabolic encephalopathy
Isolated unilateral peripheral vestibular ganglion neuritis
Bilateral lens opacification from advanced mature cataracts

explanation: In a comatose patient with an intact brainstem, the oculocephalic reflex moves the eyes opposite to head rotation because the vestibulo-ocular arc functions without cortical input. Failure indicates brainstem dysfunction (check cervical spine before testing).

stem: A 35-year-old man has severe vertigo and vomiting for 2 days after a viral illness. He has no hearing loss or tinnitus, and there are no other neurologic findings. Imaging is normal. Left vestibular neuritis is diagnosed. Which type of nystagmus is expected?

options.text: Horizontal nystagmus with fast phase beating toward the left ear
Horizontal nystagmus with fast phase beating toward the right ear
Vertical downbeat nystagmus that persists despite visual fixation
Complete absence of spontaneous or gaze-evoked ocular nystagmus
Torsional nystagmus provoked exclusively by rapid head positioning

explanation: Loss of tonic input from the left vestibular nerve causes slow drift toward the lesion with a corrective fast phase away (right-beating nystagmus), suppressed by fixation. Normal hearing separates neuritis from labyrinthitis, which also involves the cochlea.

stem: A 59-year-old man with a medullary lesion involving the medial vestibular nucleus has a persistent head tilt and difficulty holding his head upright. Which pathway most directly explains this?

options.text: Lateral vestibulospinal tract to antigravity limb extensors
Medial vestibulospinal tract to bilateral cervical neck muscles
Vestibulothalamic projection to VPL
MLF to the abducens nucleus
Rubrospinal tract to upper limb flexors

explanation: The medial vestibulospinal tract projects bilaterally to the cervical cord to control neck muscles and keep the head upright; lesions cause abnormal head position. The lateral tract controls antigravity extensors for posture.

stem: A 61-year-old man has sudden vertigo, nystagmus, right facial pain and temperature loss, right ptosis and miosis, hoarseness, dysphagia, and loss of pain and temperature in the left arm and leg. Which artery is most likely occluded?

options.text: Anterior spinal artery
Posterior cerebral artery
Basilar artery bifurcation
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
Middle cerebral artery

explanation: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome: vestibular nuclei (vertigo, nystagmus), spinal trigeminal nucleus (ipsilateral face), descending sympathetics (Horner), nucleus ambiguus (hoarseness, dysphagia), spinothalamic tract (contralateral body pain/temperature loss). Cause: PICA or vertebral artery occlusion.

stem: An 18-year-old woman has bilateral progressive hearing loss and tinnitus. Her father had hearing loss and brain tumors. MRI shows bilateral masses at the cerebellopontine angles. Mutation of which gene is most likely?

options.text: NF1 (chromosome 17)
NF2 (chromosome 22)
VHL (chromosome 3)
TSC1 (chromosome 9)
RB1 (chromosome 13)

explanation: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas define neurofibromatosis type 2, caused by loss of the NF2 tumor suppressor (merlin) on chromosome 22. Sporadic schwannomas are unilateral.

stem: A 58-year-old woman has brief episodes of vertigo on lying back with the head turned to the right. During the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, upbeating torsional nystagmus begins after a few seconds and subsides within 30 seconds; it is less intense on repeat testing. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: These features suggest a central lesion requiring urgent imaging
These features, with latency and fatigability, support BPPV of the posterior canal
These findings indicate vestibular schwannoma
These findings indicate Meniere disease
These findings indicate vestibular neuritis

explanation: Peripheral positional vertigo shows a latency of seconds, brief duration, and fatigability on repeat testing. Central positional nystagmus is immediate, persistent, non-fatigable, and often accompanied by other neurologic signs. Treatment: Epley maneuver.

stem: A 74-year-old man on antihypertensives feels lightheaded and nearly faints each time he stands up quickly. He denies any spinning sensation. Standing blood pressure falls by 30 mm Hg systolic. Which term best describes his symptom?

options.text: Vertigo resulting from peripheral vestibular dysfunction
Vertigo resulting from central pontomedullary dysfunction
Presyncope resulting from non-vestibular systemic causes
Oscillopsia resulting from bilateral vestibular loss
Tinnitus resulting from cochlear sensorineural damage

explanation:
Vertigo is a false sensation of movement/spinning from vestibular dysfunction. Lightheadedness or faintness from cardiovascular causes (orthostatic hypotension, arrhythmia) is dizziness, which is non-vestibular.


---

stem: A 68-year-old man with long-standing hypertension suddenly develops right arm and leg weakness. Examination shows increased tone, hyperreflexia, and an upgoing right plantar response. The right corner of his mouth droops and the right nasolabial fold is flattened, but he can wrinkle his forehead and close both eyes tightly. When asked to protrude his tongue, it deviates to the right. Sensation is intact. Which lesion location is most consistent with these findings?

options.text: Left internal capsule
Right facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen
Right facial and hypoglossal nuclei
Left C5 hemisection of the spinal cord
Right internal capsule

explanation: Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers run together through the internal capsule. A left lesion causes right UMN body weakness, right lower facial weakness (lower face has only contralateral corticobulbar input; the upper face is bilateral so the forehead is spared), and tongue deviation to the right (weak side; CN XII is supplied mostly by contralateral corticobulbar fibers). A right lesion (E) would produce left-sided findings; LMN lesions (B, C) wouldn't cause body UMN signs; a cord lesion (D) spares the face.

stem: A 31-year-old woman wakes with weakness of the entire right side of her face. She cannot wrinkle her forehead, raise her right eyebrow, close her right eye, or smile on the right. Her tongue protrudes in the midline. Strength and reflexes in the limbs are normal and symmetric. Which lesion best explains her findings?

options.text: Left precentral gyrus face area
Right corticobulbar fibers in the internal capsule
Right facial nerve or facial motor nucleus
Left genu of the internal capsule
Right hypoglossal nerve

explanation: Bell palsy: LMN lesion of CN VII, so all ipsilateral facial muscles (upper and lower) are weak. UMN (corticobulbar) lesions produce only contralateral lower facial weakness because upper facial motoneurons receive bilateral cortical input.

stem: A 24-year-old man sustains a complete spinal cord transection at C2 in a diving accident. After the period of spinal shock resolves, examination shows quadriplegia with increased tone, brisk patellar reflexes, sustained ankle clonus, and bilateral Babinski signs. Which best explains the hyperactive patellar reflex?

options.text: Disruption of primary afferent sensory fibers within lumbar dorsal roots
Loss of descending supraspinal inhibition onto lumbar motor neurons
Direct degenerative destruction of lumbar anterior horn motor neurons
Aberrant uninhibited synaptic transmission through lumbar dorsal columns
Post-synaptic denervation hypersensitivity of quadriceps muscle fibers

explanation: The patellar reflex (L3-L4) is a two-neuron arc within the cord and doesn't require the brain. Descending UMN tracts (reticulospinal, rubrospinal) normally suppress stretch reflex circuits and tone. Transection removes this inhibition: spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, Babinski. LMN destruction would cause areflexia.

stem: A 49-year-old woman has 10 weeks of progressive stiffness and weakness of both legs with foot dragging. She has morning headaches that worsen with coughing. Examination shows papilledema, normal arm strength, bilateral spastic leg weakness, brisk ankle reflexes, bilateral Babinski signs, and intact sensation. Face and tongue movements are normal. Which is the most likely location of the lesion?

options.text: Posterior limbs of both internal capsules
Sacral segments of the conus medullaris
Medial parasagittal cortex of both frontal lobes
Lateral convexities of both precentral gyri
Lumbosacral nerve roots of the cauda equina

explanation: The leg and foot are represented on the medial surface of the precentral gyrus (paracentral lobule), the two hemispheres' leg areas facing each other across the falx. A parasagittal meningioma can compress both: bilateral UMN leg weakness sparing arms and face; headache and papilledema reflect raised ICP. Conus and cauda equina lesions give LMN findings.

stem: A 58-year-old man with atherosclerosis has sudden left arm and leg weakness with increased tone and hyperreflexia. His face is spared. When he protrudes his tongue, it deviates to the right. Which is the most likely location of the lesion?

options.text: Left medial medulla
Right internal capsule
Left internal capsule
Right medial medulla
Right lateral medulla

explanation: A right medial medullary lesion damages the right hypoglossal nerve/nucleus (LMN: tongue deviates toward lesion) and the right pyramid, whose corticospinal fibers have not yet decussated (left hemiparesis with UMN signs), sparing the face. This is an alternating hemiplegia. A right internal capsule lesion (B) causes left weakness with left lower face droop and tongue deviating LEFT.

stem: A 5-year-old unvaccinated girl develops fever followed 2 days later by asymmetric weakness of the right leg. Examination shows markedly reduced right quadriceps strength with decreased tone, fasciculations, and an absent right patellar reflex. Sensation is normal and the plantar response is flexor. Which best describes the lesion and the spinal roots tested by the absent reflex?

options.text: Upper motoneuron lesion; L3-L4
Lower motoneuron lesion; L3-L4
Upper motoneuron lesion; S1-S2
Lower motoneuron lesion; C5-C6
Lower motoneuron lesion; S1-S2

explanation: Flaccid weakness, decreased tone, areflexia, and fasciculations with normal sensation indicate an LMN lesion (here poliovirus destroying anterior horn cells). Patellar reflex = L3-L4 (Achilles S1-S2, biceps C5-C6, triceps C6-C8). UMN lesions give spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski.

stem: A 63-year-old man has hoarseness and difficulty swallowing after resection of a skull base tumor. Examination shows drooping of the right soft palate arch, and the uvula deviates to the left when he says "ahh." The gag reflex is absent on the right. Which nerve is most likely injured?

options.text: Left vagus nerve
Left glossopharyngeal nerve
Right hypoglossal nerve
Right vagus nerve
Right trigeminal motor root

explanation: Nucleus ambiguus fibers (CN IX/X) supply palatal and pharyngeal muscles. With a right vagus lesion the right palate is weak and the intact left side pulls the uvula toward the strong side (away from the lesion). Gag reflex: CN IX afferent, CN X efferent. In CN XII and CN V LMN lesions the structure deviates TOWARD the lesion.

stem: A 20-year-old man is struck on the left side of the head with a bottle. He has decreased light touch and pinprick sensation over the left face, and when he opens his mouth the jaw deviates to the left. Which best explains the jaw deviation?

options.text: Unopposed action of the right lateral pterygoid muscle
Unopposed action of the left lateral pterygoid muscle
Weakness of the right masseter muscle
Weakness of the right temporalis muscle
A contralateral corticobulbar lesion

explanation: A left CN V LMN lesion weakens left muscles of mastication including the left lateral pterygoid. The intact right lateral pterygoid pulls the jaw forward and across to the weak (left) side: the jaw deviates toward the lesion. CN V has bilateral corticobulbar input, so a unilateral UMN lesion causes no deficit.

stem: A 28-year-old man is stabbed in the back, causing a right-sided hemisection of the spinal cord at T8. Which set of findings is expected below the level of the lesion?

options.text: Bilateral spastic weakness and bilateral loss of pain and temperature with preserved vibration sense
Left spastic weakness, left loss of vibration and proprioception, right loss of pain and temperature
Right spastic weakness, right loss of vibration and proprioception, left loss of pain and temperature
Right flaccid weakness with loss of all sensation on the right
Bilateral loss of vibration and proprioception with preserved strength

explanation: Brown-Sequard: ipsilateral UMN signs (lateral corticospinal tract, already crossed) and ipsilateral loss of touch/vibration/proprioception (dorsal columns); contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning about 2 levels below (spinothalamic fibers cross near entry). At the lesion level, ipsilateral LMN signs. (A) is anterior spinal artery infarct.

stem: A 70-year-old man with severe atherosclerosis undergoes emergency repair of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm. In the following weeks he has bilateral leg weakness with spasticity, hyperreflexia, and loss of pain and temperature sensation below the T10 level, but preserved vibration and joint position sense. Which is the most likely cause?

options.text: Occlusion of the posterior spinal arteries
Syringomyelia of the thoracic cord
Vitamin B12 deficiency
Compression of the cauda equina
Infarction of the anterior spinal artery territory

explanation: Anterior spinal artery infarction damages the anterior two-thirds of the cord: lateral corticospinal tracts (bilateral UMN signs), spinothalamic tracts (pain/temperature loss), and anterior horn cells at the level (LMN signs). Dorsal columns (posterior spinal arteries) are spared. Posterior spinal artery infarct and B12 deficiency affect dorsal columns; syrinx causes a suspended pain/temperature loss.

stem: A 40-year-old man develops severe low back pain radiating down both legs after lifting a heavy box. He now has numbness of the perineum and inner thighs and difficulty urinating. Which additional finding is most likely on examination?

options.text: Spastic paraparesis with hyperactive patellar reflexes and extensor plantars
Dissociated sensory loss with preserved proprioception and intact reflexes
Loss of vibration and joint position sense with preserved motor strength
Flaccid paraparesis with diminished Achilles reflexes and decreased anal tone
Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the lumbar level

explanation: Cauda equina syndrome: compression of lumbosacral roots (peripheral LMN axons) produces radicular pain, saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, and LMN signs (flaccid weakness, hypotonia, hyporeflexia). Surgical emergency. Conus medullaris lesions give more bilateral, sacral-predominant findings with UMN features and less radicular pain.

stem: Roughly 10% of corticospinal fibers do not decussate in the medullary pyramids and instead descend ipsilaterally in the cord. Which describes this component?

options.text: Lateral rubrospinal tract
Lateral corticospinal tract
Anterior corticospinal tract
Lateral vestibulospinal tract
Descending corticobulbar tract

explanation: About 90% of corticospinal fibers decussate at the pyramids to form the lateral corticospinal tract (limb control). The remaining ~10% descend uncrossed as the anterior corticospinal tract, crossing at spinal levels, controlling axial muscles; clinically minor.

stem: A right-sided stroke in the internal capsule causes left hemiparesis, but a right-sided hemisection of the cervical spinal cord causes right-sided spastic weakness. Which best explains this difference?

options.text: Corticospinal fibers decussate in the anterior white commissure of the cord
Corticospinal fibers decussate within the posterior limb of internal capsule
Corticospinal fibers synapse on lower motor neurons before exiting the brain
Corticospinal fibers decussate in the medulla prior to entering the cord
Corticospinal fibers descend ipsilaterally through the entire spinal cord

explanation: Because most corticospinal fibers cross at the pyramidal decussation, UMN lesions above it (cortex, capsule, brainstem) cause contralateral weakness, whereas lesions below it (spinal cord) cause ipsilateral weakness. Cord lesions also spare the face.

stem: A 60-year-old man 3 months after a left hemispheric stroke has a right arm that resists rapid passive extension at the elbow, with resistance greatest at the start of movement and then giving way. Slow movement meets less resistance. Which best describes this finding?

options.text: Velocity-dependent spasticity with loss of stretch reflex inhibition
Velocity-independent lead-pipe rigidity from extrapyramidal disease
Flaccid muscle hypotonia from anterior horn lower motor neuron loss
Cogwheel rigidity with tremor from substantia nigra degeneration
Paratonic Gegenhalten resistance from diffuse frontal lobe disease

explanation: UMN spasticity is velocity-dependent (greater resistance with faster passive movement), often clasp-knife, from loss of descending inhibition (reticulospinal/rubrospinal) of stretch reflexes. Basal ganglia rigidity (lead-pipe/cogwheel) is not velocity-dependent.

stem: A patient with chronic hemiparesis walks by swinging the right leg outward in a semicircle. The right elbow is held flexed with the wrist and fingers flexed, and the right knee is held extended. Increased tone is predominantly present in which muscle groups?

options.text: Upper limb extensors and lower limb flexors
Upper limb flexors and lower limb extensors
Upper and lower limb flexors only
Axial muscles only
Face and tongue muscles

explanation: UMN spasticity is direction-dependent: in the upper limb flexors are more affected (flexed elbow, wrist, fingers); in the lower limb extensors are more affected (extended knee, plantar-flexed foot), producing a circumducting gait.

stem: A 9-month-old infant has normal development. When the lateral sole of the foot is stroked, the great toe extends and the other toes fan out. Which is the best interpretation?

options.text: Cerebral palsy
Lower motor neuron lesion
Cervical cord compression
Brown-Sequard syndrome
A normal finding for age

explanation: An extensor (upgoing) plantar response (Babinski) is normal in infants because the corticospinal tract is incompletely myelinated; it normally disappears by about 12-24 months. Later it indicates a UMN lesion.

stem: On examination of a patient with chronic myelopathy, abrupt passive dorsiflexion of the ankle triggers 6 rhythmic beats of plantar flexion that persist while the stretch is held. This finding is most consistent with which of the following?

options.text: Lower motor neuron lesion with loss of anterior horn cells
Sensory polyneuropathy with loss of large myelinated fibers
Upper motor neuron lesion with a hyperactive stretch reflex
Neuromuscular junction disorder with impaired acetylcholine
Cerebellar hemisphere lesion with ipsilateral kinetic tremor

explanation: Clonus (repetitive rhythmic contractions after sudden stretch, usually at the ankle) reflects a hyperactive stretch reflex from loss of descending inhibition: a UMN sign. LMN lesions cause hyporeflexia and flaccidity.

stem: A 48-year-old man has neck pain radiating down the lateral arm, weak elbow flexion, and a diminished biceps reflex. Which spinal roots are most likely compressed?

options.text: C3-C4
C5-C6
C7-C8
L3-L4
S1-S2

explanation: The biceps reflex tests C5-C6 (triceps C6-C8, patellar L3-L4, Achilles S1-S2). Reduced reflex with weak elbow flexion indicates an LMN (root) lesion at C5-C6, typically a C5-C6 disc herniation.

stem: After a pelvic fracture, a patient has an absent anal wink reflex. The reflex arc tests which spinal segments?

options.text: L1-L2
L3-L4
S1-S2
S3-S4
C5-C6

explanation: The anal wink (external anal sphincter contraction on perianal stroking) is mediated by S3-S4 via the pudendal nerve. Cremasteric L1-L2, Achilles S1-S2, patellar L3-L4, biceps C5-C6.

stem: After a left frontal stroke, a 70-year-old man cannot demonstrate how to snap his fingers or brush his teeth on command. Strength, tone, reflexes, and sensation are normal. Which structure is most likely damaged?

options.text: Primary motor cortex
Premotor cortex or supplementary motor area
Posterior limb of the internal capsule
Cerebellar vermis
Anterior horn of the spinal cord

explanation: The premotor cortex and supplementary motor area plan and store learned movements. Lesions cause apraxia: inability to perform learned tasks despite normal strength, tone, and sensation. Primary motor cortex lesions cause contralateral weakness.

stem: A 66-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation has sudden weakness and spasticity of the right leg and foot, with only mild right arm weakness and normal face and tongue function. Which artery is most likely occluded?

options.text: Anterior cerebral artery
Middle cerebral artery
Posterior cerebral artery
Basilar artery
Anterior spinal artery

explanation: The leg and foot lie on the medial surface of the motor cortex (paracentral lobule), supplied by the ACA. ACA infarct: contralateral leg weakness > arm with face spared. The MCA supplies the lateral convexity (face and arm).

stem: A 62-year-old man has sudden right arm weakness with hyperreflexia, right lower facial droop, and tongue deviation to the right. He understands commands but can only say "no, no." Which vessel is most likely involved?

options.text: Right anterior cerebral artery
Left posterior cerebral artery
Left middle cerebral artery
Right middle cerebral artery
Basilar artery

explanation: The precentral gyrus face and hand areas and Broca area lie on the lateral hemisphere (MCA). A left MCA infarct causes right face and arm UMN weakness with non-fluent aphasia (comprehension intact).

stem: A 65-year-old man with long-standing hypertension has sudden left face, arm, and leg weakness of equal severity with increased tone. There is no sensory loss, aphasia, or neglect. Which is the most likely location and vessel?

options.text: Precentral gyrus motor cortex; anterior cerebral artery branches
Midbrain cerebral peduncle; posterior cerebral artery branches
Medullary pyramid; anterior spinal artery and vertebral branches
Posterior limb of internal capsule; lenticulostriate arteries
Cervical spinal cord; anterior spinal artery penetrating branches

explanation: A lacunar infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule (lenticulostriate branches of the MCA; hypertensive small-vessel disease) causes pure motor hemiparesis of face, arm, and leg because the tightly packed corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers are interrupted together, with no sensory loss or cortical signs.

stem: A 55-year-old man has acute basilar artery occlusion. He is awake and aware but quadriplegic, mute, and unable to move his eyes horizontally; he can blink and move his eyes vertically on command. Which best describes the lesion?

options.text: Bilateral medial medullary infarcts
Bilateral ventral pontine infarction
Bilateral internal capsule lacunes
Bilateral occipital infarcts
Midbrain tegmental hemorrhage

explanation: Locked-in syndrome: bilateral ventral pontine infarction (basilar artery) interrupts corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers while sparing the tegmentum (consciousness) and midbrain vertical gaze centers. Patients communicate by vertical eye movements and blinking.

stem: A 64-year-old man has right ptosis, a dilated right pupil, the right eye deviated down and out, and left arm and leg weakness with hyperreflexia. Which lesion location is most likely?

options.text: Cavernous sinus involving oculomotor and ophthalmic divisions
Superior orbital fissure involving oculomotor and abducens nerves
Midbrain tegmentum involving red nucleus and medial lemniscus
Substantia nigra and oculomotor nucleus in dorsal midbrain
Ventral midbrain involving CN III fascicles and cerebral peduncle

explanation: Weber syndrome (medial midbrain): CN III fascicle damage (ipsilateral ptosis, eye down and out, dilated pupil) plus the adjacent cerebral peduncle (corticospinal fibers: contralateral hemiparesis). Alternating hemiplegia: cranial nerve findings ipsilateral, body weakness contralateral.

stem: A 57-year-old man has right facial paralysis involving the forehead and mouth, with an inability to close the right eye, plus left arm and leg weakness with hyperreflexia. Which lesion location is most likely?

options.text: Left ventral caudal pons
Right ventral caudal pons
Right internal capsule
Right medial medulla
Right cerebral peduncle

explanation: Right ventral caudal pons: damages the CN VII fascicle (ipsilateral LMN facial palsy including the forehead) and corticospinal fibers in the basis pontis before decussation (left hemiparesis): alternating hemiplegia.

stem: After blunt head trauma, a 30-year-old man has vertical double vision that is worst when he looks down and to the left while descending stairs. The right eye cannot turn downward when adducted. Which muscle is most likely weak?

options.text: Right superior oblique
Right inferior oblique
Right lateral rectus
Right medial rectus
Right superior rectus

explanation: CN IV supplies the superior oblique, which depresses the adducted eye. Weakness causes vertical diplopia worse looking down and inward (stairs, reading). Commonly injured by head trauma because of its long intracranial course. Test: look medially, then down.

stem: A 40-year-old man with headaches and papilledema has horizontal diplopia. The right eye is turned inward at rest and cannot abduct. Which nerve is involved?

options.text: Right oculomotor nerve
Right trochlear nerve
Right abducens nerve
Left abducens nerve
Right facial nerve

explanation: CN VI (caudal pons nucleus) supplies the lateral rectus; palsy causes inward deviation and horizontal diplopia worse on gaze toward the affected side. Because of its long course, CN VI is a classic false-localizing sign of raised intracranial pressure.

stem: After a lymph node biopsy in the right posterior cervical triangle, a patient has a drooping right shoulder and weakness of the right shoulder shrug. Which additional function would be impaired?

options.text: Turning the head to the right
Turning the head to the left
Tongue protrusion
Swallowing
Jaw opening

explanation: CN XI supplies the trapezius (shoulder shrug) and sternocleidomastoid. Each SCM turns the head toward the opposite side, so right CN XI injury weakens turning the head to the left, along with a drooping, weak right shoulder.

stem: A 52-year-old man has slurred speech. The left side of his tongue is atrophic with visible fasciculations, and the tongue deviates to the left on protrusion. Which lesion is most likely?

options.text: Left hypoglossal nerve lower motor neuron lesion
Right hypoglossal nerve lower motor neuron lesion
Right corticobulbar tract upper motor neuron lesion
Left corticobulbar tract upper motor neuron lesion
Left glossopharyngeal nerve lower motor neuron lesion

explanation: Atrophy and fasciculations indicate an LMN lesion of the left hypoglossal nerve/nucleus; weak genioglossus on that side lets the tongue deviate toward the lesion. UMN (corticobulbar) lesions cause deviation toward the weak side without atrophy or fasciculations.

stem: A patient has had two lacunar strokes, one in each hemisphere, with progressive dysarthria and dysphagia. Which finding best supports pseudobulbar palsy rather than bulbar palsy due to LMN disease?

options.text: Tongue atrophy with fasciculations
Absent gag reflex
Absent jaw jerk
Flaccid palate
Brisk jaw jerk with emotional lability

explanation: Pseudobulbar palsy (bilateral corticobulbar lesions): dysarthria and dysphagia with UMN features (spastic tongue, brisk jaw jerk, pathologic laughing/crying) without atrophy or fasciculations. Bulbar palsy (LMN): flaccid tongue, atrophy, fasciculations, absent gag.

stem: A 68-year-old man has a left internal capsule stroke. His jaw opens in the midline, the palate elevates symmetrically, the uvula is midline, and shoulder shrug is normal. Which best explains the sparing of these functions?

options.text: Corticobulbar fibers do not project to these nuclei
These muscles are supplied only by spinal nerves
The lesion must have been in the cerebellum
These nuclei receive bilateral corticobulbar input
Uncrossed input is exclusive

explanation: Corticobulbar fibers innervate the trigeminal motor nucleus, nucleus ambiguus (IX/X), and CN XI bilaterally, so a unilateral corticobulbar lesion leaves jaw, palate, pharynx, and shoulder function intact. Only the lower face and tongue (largely contralateral input) are affected.

stem: When the right posterior pharynx is touched, a patient has no gag; when the left side is touched, the palate elevates and the patient gags normally. Palatal elevation on saying "ahh" is symmetric. Which nerve is most likely damaged?

options.text: Right glossopharyngeal nerve afferents
Right vagus nerve motor efferents
Left glossopharyngeal nerve afferents
Left vagus nerve motor efferents
Right hypoglossal nerve efferents

explanation: The gag reflex: CN IX afferent, CN X (nucleus ambiguus) efferent. Absent gag only on right-sided stimulation with normal palatal movement elsewhere localizes the lesion to the right afferent limb (CN IX).

stem: A 28-year-old man has a bilateral cape-like loss of pain and temperature over the shoulders and arms with preserved light touch and vibration, and atrophy of the intrinsic hand muscles. MRI shows a cervical syrinx. Which structures are damaged?

options.text: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
Posterior dorsal roots and dorsal column tracts
Posterior inferior cerebellar artery territory
Anterior white commissure and anterior horns
Anterior spinal roots and cauda equina fibers

explanation: Syringomyelia (often with a Chiari I malformation) damages crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure: bilateral cape-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved light touch (dorsal columns). It expands into the anterior horns, causing LMN weakness and atrophy of the hands.

stem: A 61-year-old strict vegan has numbness and tingling in his feet, a wide-based gait, loss of vibration and proprioception, spastic leg weakness, brisk reflexes, and Babinski signs. Which spinal cord tracts are involved?

options.text: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
Anterior horn cells and ventral spinal rootlets
Spinothalamic tracts and dorsal horn laminae
Cauda equina and lumbosacral spinal roots
Conus medullaris and anterior spinal artery

explanation: Vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia, nitrous oxide, malabsorption) causes subacute combined degeneration: dorsal columns (loss of vibration/proprioception, sensory ataxia) plus lateral corticospinal tracts (spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski). Megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils is the hematologic clue.

stem: A 55-year-old man has lightning-like leg pains, a wide-based stamping gait, a positive Romberg sign, absent ankle reflexes, and small irregular pupils that constrict with accommodation but not to light. Which structures are primarily affected?

options.text: Lateral corticospinal tracts and anterior horns
Anterior spinal artery territory
Dorsal columns and dorsal roots
Conus medullaris
Central canal

explanation: Tabes dorsalis (tertiary neurosyphilis, Treponema pallidum) degenerates dorsal columns and dorsal roots: lightning pains, sensory ataxia with positive Romberg, loss of ankle reflexes (interrupted afferent limb), and Argyll-Robertson pupils (accommodate but don't react to light).

stem: A 34-year-old man has 3 days of ascending symmetric leg weakness following a diarrheal illness. Examination shows flaccid weakness and absent deep tendon reflexes with a flexor plantar response. Which best explains the areflexia?

options.text: Upper motor neuron lesion with loss of cortical inhibition
Lower motor neuron lesion interrupting spinal reflex arcs
Cerebellar vermis lesion with midline postural instability
Basal ganglia lesion with impaired striatal dopaminergic tone
Dorsal column lesion with loss of large proprioceptive fibers

explanation:
Guillain-Barre syndrome (post-infectious demyelination of peripheral nerves, e.g., after Campylobacter jejuni): ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia from interruption of the motor and sensory limbs of the reflex arc (an LMN-type deficit). CSF: high protein, normal cell count. The location of the lesion along the lower motoneuron produces similar deficits.
